subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-EFFECT OF DISC PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. In light of the worsening unemployment situation in Canada, what is the government's current assessment on the effects of the United States DISC program on unemployment in Canada? Is this program now hurting employment in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-EFFECT OF DISC PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. Leader of the Opposition realizes, one of the antidotes was the competitive tax rates for manufacturers and processors and the capital cost allowances. speechtext: A question for the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker. Given the fact that unemployment has risen to a level of 563,000 and that experts have forecast a much larger increase for the months ahead, can the Prime Minister tell us whether the government has made its own forecast of unemployment this winter, and, if so, what levels of unemployment are expected?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-GOVERNMENT FORECAST OF LEVEL- SUGGESTED INCREASE IN FUNDS FOR WINTER PROJECTS
speechtext:
On a
quarterly basis, and then publicly at the time of the budget, the government does look at the state of the economy, studies the current situation and considers the factors which might affect the future. No attempt is made to make any precise forecast.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-GOVERNMENT FORECAST OF LEVEL- SUGGESTED INCREASE IN FUNDS FOR WINTER PROJECTS
speechtext: Recognizing the need to take some kind of specific action in advance of the budget, for which we may have to wait some four weeks by which time it will be too late to do anything effective about winter unemployment, can the Minister of Finance inform the House whether or not the government will consider increasing the capital allotted to the winter projects fund? At present this is fixed at some $350 million. Would the minister consider substantially increasing this sum and making an early announcement to this effect in order that the provinces and the cities can get projects of a serious nature under way, hopefully by the latter part of the winter at least. This could have a beneficial effect on the unemployment situation.

The Minister of Labour mentioned the Prime Minister's letter to the grain companies, which said that this situation is unique, will not affect other union negotiations and is not inflationary. You, the Prime Minister of Canada, have ensured that legislative action will be taken to enforce the Dr. Neil Perry report which ensures Vancouver grain workers of a basic rate of pay amounting to $6.44 per hour.
This is $2.11 an hour more than grain inspectors are paid. I continue reading the letter:
Government inspectors who control and supervise all grain received and exported at the port of Vancouver have to receive, at least, parity with all of the Vancouver grain workers.
If we do not receive parity with all these grain workers in Vancouver, our inspectors will take the necessary action to protect our interests.
Signed: C. Lewis, Chairman, Bargaining Committee, Local 60.
It goes without saying that if the grain inspectors do not work, grain will not leave the port. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) said yesterday that management and the union had been deadlocked for over half a year and the government was forced to act. Let us examine that contention. The first meeting between management and the union was held on October 19, 1973. The fifth and final meeting was held on December 11, 1973. There were only five direct meetings during a seven-week period. Surely the minister could have exercised the options open to him and ordered that serious negotiations be undertaken. Section 164(1) one of the Canada Labour Code outlines the options available to the minister. He can notify the parties of his intention not to appoint a conciliation officer or conciliation commissioner, or he can establish a conciliation board.
Section 43 of the Canada Grain Act declares elevators to be works for the general advantage of Canada. Our railways fall under that category as well. Surely these are not idle words in the statute. The government is responsible for seeing that such works are used for the advantage of our country. We are dealing with a national problem which has become a national disgrace.
I now wish to refer to a European magazine, Point International. The edition of September 21, 1974, says the following about the Vancouver grain pile-up:
Federal politicians are behaving indecisively. Had private companies been involved, parliament would have been recalled and the proposal enforced. But farm co-operatives cannot be handled in this fashion: grain growers have long memories on polling day. Meanwhile the country, which needs massive grain exports to keep its economy healthy, is severely threatened.
In a situation such as the Vancouver grain tie-up, I feel great unease at the government's reliance upon advisers who operate in the theoretical rather than the practical field and whose advice appears to be adding to the mounting mess rather than alleviating it. I hope the Minister of Labour will consider this when he appoints an industrial inquiry commission, because so far in this situation we have suffered from a classic case of legal overkill.
On October 19, 1972, the former agreement was ratified. Its duration was December 1, 1971 to November 30, 1973. The increase granted was approximately 40 cents an hour, or 9 per cent across the board. In the current disagreement, the first meeting was held on October 19, 1973. The fifth and final meeting between management and union was held on December 11. That was the end of our so-called collective bargaining. On February 15, 1974, the
Grain Handlers' Strike
Minister of Labour appointed Dr. G. N. Perry as a conciliation commissioner, and I quote-
-to assist the parties to the dispute in revising the collective agreement.
His terms of reference were all wrong. However, the government took his report as a settlement without knowing what it was all about.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
I quote as follows from the preamble to Dr. Perry's report:
-the recommendations which follow can hardly be expected to do more than indicate a series of intermediate changes with which both parties may be able to associate themselves as they try to conclude a settlement in a difficult year.
The Perry report does not discuss the basic issues at all. They are productivity, efficiency and incentives. The real issue is not to do something that will add to the inflationary pressure in the country, but to do something that will move more grain through export positions at the lowest possible cost per bushel. With trains and ships operating around the clock, seven days a week, steps must be taken to put grain terminals on the same basis. It is obvious, too, that we must move toward a system whereby clean, ready to export grain is moved to export positions.
I am certain of one thing: we will not get increased productivity by parliament legislating this settlement. On May 23, 1974, the government took action under section 181 to make a strike or lock-out illegal until after the election. There is doubt about the legality of the government's action, and the sloppy staff work showed up when they omitted from the order the terminal owned by James Richardson. The title of Bill C-12 is "An act to provide for the resumption of grain handling operations on the west coast of Canada". I would like the House to understand that two terminals one operated by the Alberta Wheat Pool in Victoria and a terminal in Prince Rupert have operated throughout the Vancouver shut-down.
Ministers of the Crown made it clear that unless the parties in the meantime reached agreement, a settlement would be legislated in accordance with the commissioner's recommendations. Any chance of effective and meaningful bargaining ended absolutely when the Minister of Labour said during the election campaign that the government would, if re-elected, legislate implementation of the report. This promise was reiterated later by the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. There remained a great-deal of ground for negotiation.
On August 1, 1974, the government of Canada made two rather dramatic moves in the grain business. They granted the companies an unprecedented increase in the tariff for both country elevator operation and for terminal operation. This increase was granted by order in council P C. 1974-1702, dated July 30, 1974, to be effective August 1, 1974. At the same time, the government reduced the payment for number one bread wheat to the western farmer from $3.75 to $2.25 a bushel, a reduction of some 40 per cent. On August 8, the no strike, no lock-out order expired. On August 23, 1974, strikes plus lock-outs, completely shut down the Vancouver grain terminals. The greatest grain exporting port in a hungry world sat idle. Works for the general advantage indeed!

October 8, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
Instead of reminding the grain companies of their responsibilities, I suggest this government should have looked to their own responsibilities in this matter. It must be obvious even to this government that third party intervention is necessary in labour disputes right from the start, and I do not necessarily mean government intervention. In the case before us, I suggest three or four farmers sitting in as observers would have tended to keep both parties on the track.
History tells us that almost every time the government interferes with agriculture, they spoil the market; and if the marketing is wrong, we might as well plow under all the other effort. The expansion of our grain exports and competitive strength depend more on our own efforts than on our reliance on negotiating with other countries. There are a number of actions and policies we can initiate unilaterally which will contribute to our goals of increased trade.
Our greatest need is to have a consistently dependable supply of major grain items, at competitive world prices, at seaboard. Instead, heavy-handed interference by ministers of the Crown has resulted in the present impasse. If the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board wants to nationalize the grain industry, and this is a first step, he should be honest enough to say so. I quote as follows from the Alberta Wheat Pool publication "Budget" of October 4, 1974:
G. L. Harrold, president, Alberta Wheat Pool, said in Calgary recently that a statement by labour minister, John Munro threatening nationalization of the grain handling industry is out of order and ill-timed. Public coercion of any industry by a minister of the Crown constitutes bad government. A threat to nationalize the grain handling industry, 80 per cent of which is owned by farmers, is preposterous.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
The manner of government support for the inland terminal concept, and the method by which they have supported this concept with taxpayers' money, is another example of the sort of pressure they have been putting on western grain companies. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board is guilty of treating the grain companies like political parties. He made one very bad mistake when he tried publicly to pressure the companies. If he wanted to give them hell, he should have done it in a private office.
It was common knowledge at the meetings of the minister and company presidents that the minister had no idea what was contained in the Perry report. This explains why the government is now backing away from settlement based on that report and why they have to appoint an all-powerful referee under section 7 of the legislation. How can we, in good conscience, support this bill when we do not know what it will mean to either party?
One question that could be asked is, why did the Minister of Labour take the conciliation officer route rather than appoint a board of arbitration? I would also like to know why the Richardson terminal at Vancouver was exempt from the order in council which barred a lock-out or strike. One of the most disgraceful aspects of this whole situation was the effort of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board to try to drive a wedge between members and management of the western grain companies. Fortunately, he failed. He then, obviously, misadvised the Prime

Minister by suggesting that grain producers would apply pressure to their companies to settle. This did not happen.
The government has done nothing to create goodwill between the parties-and goodwill is needed desperately. The responsibility for supporting inflationary pressures rests upon the shoulders of the Trudeau government. They created the mess in the grain industry at Vancouver and they should pick up the tab for demurrage, now at least $10 million. In the mind of the public, this government has created the myth that bread wheat has been bringing the producer $6 or more a bushel. However, we shall find out in January upon receipt of the final payment, which I judge will bring a total return to our farmers of some $4 a bushel.
The government is all in favour of acting on the basis of the Perry Report, a settlement amounting to an increase of some 60 per cent, because the farmers will pay the full shot and increase the government's take via taxes. At the same time, the federal government, through the Treasury Board, is offering its grain employees in Vancouver, highly-trained inspectors and weighmen, only 6 per cent, although, as I have said, these people are on a lower pay scale than the grain handlers by some $2 an hour.
So, Mr. Speaker, there we have it. Make the grain growers pay the full shot for an expensive labour settlement, while the government increases the tariff for handling the grain and reduces the initial price to farmers by 40 per cent: is this the way to serve the national interest and the interest of Canadian citizens? The Prime Minister speaks of the grain companies doing a disservice to farmers. The disservice to farmers is strictly the responsibility of the government in this situation. The present government, which gave the western farmers the LIFT program and then asked the taxpayers of Canada for $200 million for hopper cars to move the grain, lets these same hopper cars sit idle. Over 200 miles of loaded boxcars are in the western division right now; over 40 million bushels of grain are stored in railroad cars. To use the government's own words, it is a mess. Mr. Speaker, it is a mounting mess. We not only need the grain moving for the next two months, but for the next 20 years.
Surely it is a reflection of an unjust society when a government will permit so much economic power to rest in the hands of so few people. It is the broader question that the government should be addressing, the problem of pockets of economic power. This is only the first labour problem with which this House will have to deal. Some mechanism must be found to take these issues out of parliament.
It may be reasonable to let the grain handlers catch up with other unions, but when does the primary producer get a chance to catch up? In Canadian agriculture we want a situation in which our farmers have confidence in maintaining planned expansion, while consumers can obtain food at fair prices. What we have from the present government is a situation in which high market prices are combined with lack of confidence in the industry. We have the worst of both worlds for the consumer and the producer.
Since January last the government has watched the west coast grain industry going down the drain. Having
October 8, 1974

let the situation slide for three months after the election, they now base legislation on a disputed, one-man report, with no assurance of increased productivity. In the minds of a good many of my constituents, the government's handling of the west coast grain situation has been a worse risk than hail, rust or grasshoppers.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party has always been extremely reluctant to impose a settlement in labour disputes by arbitrary legislation. Ever since Abraham Lincoln freed the slaves, it has been held on this continent that no one has the right to set the price at which a person shall be compelled to work in our society. For this reason, it has been a tradition in Canada that the matter of determining the price of an individual's labour should be settled by negotiation and by the process of free collective bargaining.
This process works in 99 per cent of the cases which are negotiated each year, and we hear very little about it. But there are times when the two parties in a dispute are not able to reach a mutually acceptable settlement with respect to wages, hours of work and conditions of labour. When this happens, a stoppage of work ensues and in some cases the stoppage goes on for a considerable length of time. The main victims are usually the employers, who lose business, and the employees who lose wages.
There are times when a work stoppage affects not only employers and employees, but the entire economy. We are now considering a labour dispute of this description. We face a strike which has been going on for some six weeks, a strike which is having an adverse effect on the economy and, in particular, on the well-being of the wheat producers of western Canada. We in the NDP are supporting this bill because we believe it is necessary to intervene in the interest of those who produce wheat in western Canada.
It is now more than ten months since the old agreement between the grain handlers' union and the grain handling companies expired. The work stoppage has gone on for some six weeks. The main losers in this industrial conflict have been the western farmers. In a letter dated August 23 to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, the chairman of the Wheat Board summed up his conclusions as follows:
In summary it can be fairly stated:
(a)	Each day that the strike goes on will cost Canada $5 million in lost sales. A seven-week strike will cost approximately $200 million.
(b)	Demurrage charges will total approximately $10 million
(c)	Canada's reputation as a dependable source of food supplies has already been damaged. A strike now may well destroy that reputation.
(d)	There will be a loss of ability by Canada to meet world emergency for food needs.
We need not take all of that statement at its face value. Normally, we would lose sales. However, the shortage of grain in the world is such is that we shall probably recoup the losses in sales. I believe that if the strike is satisfactorily settled, the chances are that we shall also recoup our reputation as a dependable supplier. On the other hand, turning to points (b) and (d), there can be no doubt, first
Grain Handlers' Strike
of all, that the farmers of the prairie provinces have already lost $10 million in demurrage payments which will have to be made by the Wheat Board and which will come out of their final payment; and, second, there can be no doubt that we are not at the present time making a responsible contribution toward meeting the food needs of the world.
The latest report of the World Food and Agricultural Organization indicates that right now the world is short of about six million tons of grain. Hungry people go to bed night after night without having had enough to eat. Canada has always prided itself on having made a major contribution to feeding the hungry world. Therefore, it seems to those of us in this party that the time has come to bring this matter to a conclusion. As a matter of fact, it is difficult for me to understand why the government did not move sooner than it has. Those two Dead End Kids, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), announced that unless this matter could be settled quickly, the government would call parliament into session and pass legislation implementing the Perry report. But when the companies refused to accept the Perry report, nothing happened and the matter has dragged on.
The Minister of Labour then began to say in his press statements that parliament should not really be enforcing decisions of this kind. The government should either have kept out of the matter or called parliament together and ended it, saving the farmers of western Canada the millions of dollars they have already lost in demurrage charges, and also enabling us to meet our commitments to our customers and get grain into the markets of the world.
My good friend, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), said yesterday that this bill does nothing to deal with the basic grievances. I admit there will still be many grievances left, but the fact is that this bill will do two things which are of vital importance to this country. The first is that it will get the grain moving and save the farmers of western Canada large sums of money since charges to date now amount to three times what it would have cost to settle on the basis of the Perry report. The second thing the bill will do is to offer some measure of justice to the grain handlers on the Pacific coast. Not only do we want to see this strike ended so as to stop the very serious losses being incurred by farmers in the prairie provinces; we want to see the work stoppage ended on a basis that is just, fair and equitable to the grain handlers.
It should be remembered that it was the grain companies that asked for conciliation under the Canada Labour Code. When the Perry report was brought down, the grain companies rejected it. The union indicated its willingness to accept it. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) said yesterday that the report simply was made up of suggestions. Doctor Perry was not appointed as an arbitrator, he was appointed as a conciliator and all he could make were suggestions. Since the companies were not prepared to negotiate on the basis of those suggestions, I do not think this House has any alternative but to end the strike on the basis of the recommendations of the Perry report.

October 8, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
For my friends in the Progressive Conservative Party to say that this settlement is inflationary is, in my opinion, hypocritical humbug. I have not heard them complaining about the rising profits of the food wholesaling and retailing industry, the skyrocketing profits of the oil companies, or the increase in the price of oil to farmers. I have not heard them complaining about the drastic increase in the price of farm machinery. With the increase in the price of a combine this year alone, the average farmer will pay many times what he will be called upon to pay under this settlement-approximately one cent a bushel. Nor have I heard the official opposition talking about the increase in the price of anti-freeze and other items. The fact is, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain said yesterday in the debate, that an increase of even 5 per cent would be inflationary. It is true that any increase is inflationary.
Are my friends in the Progressive Conservative Party suggesting that no increases at all should be granted? This year the cost of living has increased 11.5 per cent. We must remember that these workers will be signing a two-year agreement, which means they are guessing what the increase in the cost of living will be next year. Nobody but workers contract to sell their labour at a price, not knowing what will happen to the cost of living. I have not heard these hon. gentlemen protesting the fact that over the past year the income, in real dollar terms, of a worker in Canada has declined by $5.50 per week, or protesting the fact that the share of total national income that has gone to wage and salary earners has declined, while the share that has gone to corporations has increased. Is it now being suggested that 553 men who handle grain for five companies are to carry the burden of stopping inflation, while oil companies, banks, insurance companies and food distributing agencies continue to pile up profits? Surely this is the height of absurdity.
The farmers themselves have had very substantial increases in their prices; and they needed them, because for decades in this country farmers have been producing food at the cost of production and in some years at less than the cost of production. We have said that instead of freezing prices and wages we should try to iron-out inequities. If any group has suffered from inequities, it is the farming population, particularly the grain producers of western Canada. They received an increase and were entitled to an increase, and no one is objecting to their getting that increase. But surely we cannot say that everybody must mark time even though the cost of living is increasing.
The real argument here is not whether this is going to cost, as the grain handling companies say, an additional 61 per cent, though now they are talking about 48 per cent and the minister says the increase in wages is about 15 per cent. You can have endless arguments about statistics, but that is not the point at issue at all. The real point at issue is whether these 553 men should be discriminated against, whether they should be working for $1.25 an hour less than the dock workers beside whom they work. May I say that they work under much more hazardous conditions, much less healthy conditions, than do the dock workers; and they work beside men who have a pension plan while they have none.

The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain was quite correct when he spoke of frustration and lack of communication between workers and employers in the grain handling industry on the Pacific coast. What are these men asking for? They are not asking for the moon. They are asking to be brought, step by step, up to parity with the longshoremen beside whom they work. This agreement will not give them parity with the longshoremen; they will still be getting 25 cents an hour less in wages and they will still be getting 25 cents an hour less in their contributions to the pension plan. But at least it will bring them close to the longshoremen, and I say they are entitled to that.
In my constituency there are many hundred longshoremen and I know many of them. I can tell this House that they do not live the life of Riley. They are not living in affluence. I suggest to the grain handling companies that if the wages they are paying are so low that will it take a 48 per cent, a 68 per cent or any other increase to bring them up to parity with the longshoremen, that is not something of which to be proud. These men are entitled to a comparable wage and to parity with the men alongside whom they work. They are entitled to a pension plan for the first time. Any employer, in this day and age, who does not have a pension plan for his employees has nothing to boast about.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Any
company that allows the type of working conditions which have obtained in the elevators at Vancouver ought to be taking a very serious look at its public and employee relations.
There is no doubt that what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain said yesterday is correct: implementing the Perry report will not settle all the problems. Of course, there will be many other problems. But if this legislation gets grain moving, removes the sense of legitimate grievance which these men have, convinces them they are going to be allowed to move toward parity and makes it possible to establish better relations, then I say we will have taken the first worth-while step. It goes without saying that the secret of successful management-labour relations is to remove any sense of injustice and to help the men feel they are being treated fairly and equitably as compared with their fellow workers.
I am glad the government is going to set up a public inquiry to look into grain handling facilities. Let me make one suggestion to the government. It should not only look into grain handling facilities but into grain transportation facilities in this country. Our farmers are probably the most modernized and efficient producers of grain in the world, but they are serviced by one of the most inefficient and obsolete grain transportation and handling systems in the world. If the government considers the coal handling and transportation facilities on the Pacific coast, comparing them with how we handle grain, it will understand why we have faced these difficulties in the last few years.
Let me refer again to the letter dated August 23 which the chairman of the Wheat Board sent to the minister, in
October 8, 1974

which he pointed out that the Wheat Board has firm commitments which will require 700 cars per day. He said they were now getting 140 to 180 cars. I can recall flying over Vancouver harbour time and again and seeing 19 or 20 ships waiting, not because there was a strike but because grain supplies were not coming through on the railroad. If the government is going to look into grain handling facilities-and it should in order that they will become more efficient and more effective in handling grain-it will be of little value unless the government is prepared at the same time to look into the transportation system which in this country is obsolete and is still using outmoded methods for both the transportation and distribution of grain.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do not suggest for a moment that the passing of this bill will solve all the problems in respect of handling grain, but we in this party support it. We support it because we think that by ending the strike we will be assisting the farmers of the prairie provinces. I would point out that on the basis of what this strike has already cost the farmers, they have paid the total cost of this agreement at least three times over. We are supporting this bill because we think that in justice and equity the very least we can do is take the first timid step toward putting the grain handlers on the Pacific coast on a par with their fellow workers on the docks.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in following the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), a gentleman whom I hold in great esteem, I am sorry to say that he seemed to fall into the error which other members of his party fell into during this debate, the same error which the lead speaker for his party

the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin)-condemned the government for falling into. He seemed to start off by taking sides in this dispute. That is exactly what this House is not called upon to do, and it is exactly what the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, in the debate yesterday, accused the government of doing. Of course, he was right. It is essential that all hon. members realize that we in this House are not called upon to determine whether the Perry report is right or wrong. We are called upon to pass a bill which will implement the Perry report whether it be right or wrong. The whole point, Mr. Speaker, is that the collective bargaining process has been interfered with because the government took sides, as the hon. member said yesterday.
I think it is important to commend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and his officials for the fact that the minister will appoint an industrial inquiry commission. If there is one thing on which all hon. members agree in this debate, it is that this kind of labour-management dispute affects the national interest. In his speech yesterday, the Minister of Labour admitted unequivocally that the work stoppage which has halted the shipment of Canadian grain adversely affects the Canadian interest.
Along with other members of this party, I had the privilege of meeting representatives of the grain handlers, the managers of terminals in Vancouver and, in Calgary, several of the presidents of the co-operatives. Our discussions were frank and useful and I express my appreciation
Grain Handlers' Strike
and, I believe, the appreciation of my colleagues for the co-operation we received from both management and labour.
There is no question that relations between the two sides to this dispute can be improved. On this I agree with other spokesmen in this debate. It is clear to us that neither side believed that the other was prepared to negotiate in good faith. In that atmosphere, it is difficult to come to any agreement. Perhaps an industrial inquiry commission will make recommendations which will prove helpful. It is at least a positive step, and for that I commend the minister. However, in respect of the government's handling of the situation to date there is no room for commendation, and no reason the government should expect our party to endorse its conduct by voting for this bill.
From the moment the Minister of Labour endorsed the Perry report, any hope ended of the parties reaching a settlement. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goo-dale), who made his first speech in this House yesterday, said some thoughtful things. He said some other things as well. In defence of the government, he said that the Perry report was the end product of the collective bargaining process. That, clearly, is not correct. It is not correct because Dr. Perry, clearly, did not intend his report to be the end product of collective bargaining. Let us consider what Dr. Perry said in his report. I quote from a letter to the Minister of Labour, dated April 22:
-I am, therefore, submitting for your consideration some suggestions which, hopefully, might form a basis upon which the two parties could, ultimately, enter into a two-year agreement.
Dr. Perry wrote that report, in a spirit of meditation, as the basis upon which the parties could ultimately enter into an agreement. What would the report have been had he been functioning as an arbitrator? As my hon. friend said a few moments ago, we do not know and apparently never will. Apparently neither the Minister of Labour nor the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board read Dr. Perry's letter, or if they did they ignored it. Either way, they took sides in the dispute by endorsing the report and made matters worse by saying the report would be legislated by parliament if the parties could not agree. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, speaking on behalf of his party, accused the government of ineptness in publicly taking sides. He is right: it was the taking of sides which ended all hope of settlement.
It should be apparent to all hon. members that it is not the government's responsibility to take sides. Nor, I might add, is it the responsibility of hon. members to take sides. It is regrettable that the position on this matter, put so sensibly by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, was not heeded by other members of his party and members of the government. The government's action, in addition to making a farce of collective bargaining, amounted to an absolute abdication of responsibility for the national interest-which was, and is, to keep grain moving to Canada's customers abroad.
The Minister of Labour invoked the Canada Labour Code to prevent a strike taking place during the election. Why? Because of the national interest. This was admitted in the speech yesterday. The Minister of Industry, Trade

October 8, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) repeatedly has stated his concern that Canada must maintain its image as a responsible supplier. The evidence is overwhelming that this work stoppage involved the national interest. The conflicting statements made by government spokesmen, however, are quite extraordinary. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board, in mid-summer said:
We have successfully sold a tremendous amount of grain at top prices and need an all-out effort to deliver it. Not only is it in the interests of the western farmers to whom it is particularly crucial that we deliver, but in the national interest as well.
In March, 1974, Mr. G. N. Vogel, chief commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board, said:
Canada's grain transportation system has fallen down so badly that the country's reputation as a dependable supplier of grain to the world market is threatened.
On August 23, Mr. Vogel wrote to the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board as follows:
Our board urges every effort be made to effect a quick settlement of the impasse, including, if necessary, the immediate recalling of parliament.
Incredibly, in September the Minister of Labour was saying that parliament should not be recalled because the dispute was not truly national; and this after he had threatened to recall parliament and had accepted the Perry report as being the end of the matter. He said that parliament should not be recalled because the dispute was not truly national. I ask, is it any wonder that a columnist in the Financial Post called such a contention absurd? At the commencement of the complete tie-up of all grain movement in August, the Minister of Labour said:
-the farmers aren't hurting.
He went on to say:
Everybody is concerned about delays in delivery, but it's a seller's market. Besides, those who have negotiated grain contracts with Canada are aware of the Canadian way of handling labour disputes and that we have no control over port movement-those countries know that.
The stance of the government became even more incredible when the Minister of Labour flew to Vancouver in the first week of September. He did not speak to management or to labour. He held a press conference, and as suddenly as he appeared he disappeared. He said:
I am, quite frankly, trying through you and the public to make a plea to inject some rationality into this dispute-
The public was confused about whether there was any national interest in the strike. It was confused about the government's position, and was so sure there was no rationality in the government's position that the government truly looked ridiculous. As one columnist said-
As a result, labour minister John Munro stands undressed. His colleague, Wheat Board minister Otto Lang, is almost as naked.
It is quite clear that the strange antics of the Minister of Labour and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board had created an impasse, having-at least by insinuation- threatened the recall of parliament to legislate the Perry report. Neither side could budge. Why should they? All this time the Minister of Labour was asking the parties to somehow continue negotiations. Negotiations toward what end? Why should the union negotiate? Why should the co-ops negotiate? The government's clumsy and ill-consid-

ered statements guaranteed no settlement short of parliamentary action.
Yesterday the hon. member for Assiniboia said that the official opposition was not very concerned about restorting the movement of grain. Apart from the fact that such a statement is nonsense, the hon. member seems to have a very selective memory of what has happened. The government, despite all the conflicting statements, did believe the grain stoppage affected the national interest. The government, quite properly, invoked the Canada Labour Code and prevented a strike before the election.
I say that the government was wrong in endorsing one side's position. Having done so, and at the same time having threatened to recall parliament to end the dispute, the government had a clear duty to maintain consistency and do exactly what it threatened to do. Having bungled the collective bargaining process, parliament should have been recalled by the government.
Once the government stopped a strike in May because of the national interest, it is ludicrous to attempt later to say that it was not a matter of national interest. From the time the election was over, the responsibility for slow-downs and then complete cessation of all grain shipment rests solely with the government. This government had a duty to act in the national interest, and it has failed utterly to do so.
I have no doubt the Minister of Labour was sincere when he threatened to recall parliament. I have no doubt he was overruled by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). But it is fair to ask what other government members were doing to persuade the Prime Minister to meet the government's obligation to the national interest. And, especially, what were the Liberal members from the Vancouver area doing? They knew that the grain stoppage was affecting the national interest. They knew the grain stoppage should have been ended, no matter with which side they sympathized, and they knew-or should have known- that only parliament could get the grain moving again. As I said earlier, the hon. member for Assiniboia said some thoughtful things. He concluded his speech by saying: "We must heighten our resolve to find a better way".
It is true that this dispute is the result of a breakdown in communication and understanding between the parties. The union has stated its desire to meet with management to discuss a better way to move grain, and I believe management is prepared to do that. The union expressed, I believe, a sincere desire to solve the problems of productivity, incentive, efficiency and communication. Some of these matters may be resolved by the industrial inquiry commission. But underlying all this is a serious defect in our approach to negotiations in cases involving the national interest or, for that matter, essential services.
Collective bargaining proceeds on the assumption that each side has two traditional weapons, lock-out and strike. But in cases of national interest, overriding public interest or essential services-all such terms are used-both parties are asked to negotiate knowing that these economic weapons are not really available, or at least are available for only a very short time. I have said before that the right to strike or the right to lock-out in such cases is largely illusory. As a consequence, one side or the other can use the inevitable fact of parliamentary intervention to what
October 8, 1974

they perceive to be their own advantage. The Woods report tried to deal with this problem by recommending an industrial disputes commission. Recently, the Minister of Labour has been talking about a series of discussions with labour, industry and other groups to find a solution.
The traditional view that these disputes are settled in free bargaining and are determined by the relative strengths of the parties was put by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) last August 31 in the debate concerning the railworkers. He said:
How is the level of wages established? Is it according to a certain rule of justice, as I heard yesterday? No. It is according to the strength of each party. I have been in that trade all my life. I was involved in certain strikes where the justice of cause was very clear, and we lost. I was involved in others where it was less evident, and we won. Why? Because we were weak in the first case and strong in the second. This is the way disputes are settled. They are not settled according to certain criteria or principles known or accepted by everybody. It is free bargaining.
That has been the traditional view, Mr. Speaker, but in my submission it is old fashioned and outdated. Mr. R. C. Smith, chairman of the non-operators negotiating committee, on June 19, 1973, said the following to the conciliation board:
It may be said that the last two collective agreements have resulted from collective bargaining without the intrusion of parliament. Nothing is further from the truth. We are never removed from the shadow of parliament which hovers over us and which, by its very presence, successfully protects the interests of management.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me there is a lesson to be learned from this impasse. It is clear that the system of collective bargaining involving management and labour in those parts of the economy which affect the public interest or essential services, is not working.
The fact is that where the national interest is vital, the traditional weapons are not effective but we continue to negotiate as if they were. We are operating under a myth and, until we face this fact, we will be unlikely to reach a solution satisfactory to the parties or the public interest.
Yesterday, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) said in reference to this dispute that if he had to do it all over again he could not see how he could do it differently. I am sorry to hear that, Mr. Speaker, because there was a different way to do it and there still is a better way to do it.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest to the Minister of Labour that he consult with the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) and, to use his words, "heighten his resolve to find a better way".

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me to congratulate you on your appointment to your high office. Mr. Deputy Speaker, may I also congratulate you.
My colleagues, and particularly the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), have put forward very constructive and positive suggestions about the eventual solution of this labour-management dispute that is so central to the problems that exist in Canada today. I am not going to take up your time by repeating the things that have been said. I will take time, however, to express another viewpoint that I think is paramount,
Grain Handlers' Strike
and that is to ask how we in Canada are going to solve the labour-management problems facing us.
It is a fact that higher prices cause higher wages and higher wages push up prices. From my sphere of business, one cent of direct cost on a consumer item at the manufacturing level that is not absorbed through productivity, becomes five cents at the consumer level. Higher prices cause higher wages. Higher wages do push up prices and the ferris wheel goes round and round. Where it stop, history knows only too well.
Bargaining normally comes to a halt in a major recession and breaks either the corporation or the union or both. An exception is the case of the strike lock-out with the grain workers in Vancouver. Bargaining came to a halt when two ministers of the government autocratically ordered the settlement on the basis of a report that in my opinion was never intended to be legislation. That report also contains clauses and costs to management that were not asked for by the union at the bargaining table. The autocratic action of these two ministers in ordering settlement on the terms of the Perry report finished meaningful negotiations in the dispute and made further collective bargaining under federal jurisdiction a farce and meaningless.
Was there room for ongoing negotiations in the Perry report? I say there was. Management took an exaggerated calculation and said it was going to cost them $3.03 additional on their base net figure of $4.96. The union's calculations showed $2.14. Half a cent a bushel difference in cost, and there was no further talk. This is utter madness and a disregard of the best interests of Canada.
To legislate this report sets an official government benchmark that leaves more and more people in the Canadian work force, and those on fixed incomes, further and further behind in purchasing power. This government serves well the organized monopolies which have high leverage. The fruits of this land are truly for the pockets of power under the Liberal government. Sooner or later- and I hope my effort makes it sooner-we will have to update the purchasing power of the unorganized workers in this country who make up two-thirds of the work force and who are not enjoying the fruits of collective bargaining. I am not so sure that those who are organized want them, however, because they would have to share too much of their gain.
I am from the nice, clean, straightforward world of business, Mr. Speaker. During this dispute I have spent time with management, their negotiating committee, union negotiators, the picket line and the company presidents. In all honesty, I must say that I was not impressed with the sincerity of management or the quality of the negotiations. The management negotiating unit did not indicate to me that they had a comprehension or a unit of measure for the human quotient of the present-day need of a modern work force. Management and the companies, understandably, still carry the fears and values that are rooted in the thirties. They did not show me an awareness that in Canada new values, new social concerns and new life styles now make up a significant part of this country's work force.
Since 1967 we have seen the conflict that has existed in many Canadian homes and the testing of parental author-

October 8, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
ity. We have watched youth testing the values of our established systems on our campuses and our school grounds. We have watched the establishment in our society being tested in recent years. These people are now part of the work force of Canada. They resist the old autocracy and parentalism of the establishment. Surely we know this by now. They feel they have a right to ask, why? They are intolerant of wasteful methods and tired egos. They respond to being asked to take part in the planning of new production methods, and there is proof of this in England and in West Germany. They respond to meaningful communication and to a sense of belonging in their daily work. They also want some meaning from that daily work. They are entitled to clean toilets and pleasant eating conditions and, surely, to a proper lunch period, as are others in the province of British Columbia.
Nowhere did I see, or sense, on the part of management, an appreciation of these job enrichment factors that are so important to the productivity and peace of a modern economic enterprise. You might think I am far left, speaking from a free enterprise platform, Mr. Speaker, but I want to protect this free enterprise system. I believe sincerely, from the bottom of my heart, that management today has to understand that in this era of social change, their economic unit or franchise must serve man and serve him well.
Management must serve its customers, its employees and its suppliers. If my peers in management fail in their job enrichment, comprehension, fail in their leadership and encouragement in areas of productivity, if they continually blame, not serve, their labour force, this country is surely going to be delivered to a system of state capitalism. I do not believe that state capitalism can serve man's needs and freedoms as well as enlightened leadership in a free enterprise society.
Why are not human considerations and productivity considerations part of this legislation? The government has had enough time to instil them into the bill. Let us use this senseless circumstance as the starting point for a new era in labour-management relations. Let us return to the dream that built this country. May labour and management heal their wounds and come together in meaningful dialogue after the passage of this bill. Let them be wise enough to remove the stigma of forced legislation from their dialogue. May they remember that increased wages without corresponding productivity shove up prices. Higher prices pull up wages. High interest rates further push up prices. Increased government spending increases demand. Demand increases prices. Higher prices pull up wages. Higher wages push up prices. The end of this mad, insane spiral is collapse.
The roots of inflation are political. Is the leadership we are seeing in this area deliberate? I ask members of the government to remember that their mandate in 1974 came from Upper and Lower Canada. I ask them to stop imposing their traditional, and what I call imperialistic attitudes and mistakes on Canadians of the west. We in the west are trying to build trading corridors to the Pacific. We need the government's help, and not its ill conceived interference.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the second time within two years that parliament has been asked to pass legislation forcing men back to work. It is a disagreeable task which members of parliament do not relish. If this legislation had simply provided for resumption of work and for the parties to resume collective bargaining in the best interests of the nation, it would be acceptable. Yet we, as legislators, are being asked to decide on increases in wages and other benefits without being given the full facts or the opportunity to examine witnesses from both sides. We are asked to legislate benefits arbitrarily decided by the government, without being given the facts. I respectfully submit that no member of this House is qualified to make such decisions.
I represent a constituency in Saskatchewan which depends primarily upon grain production. This year, 1974, has been a tragic one for prairie grain producers who have been plagued with spring flooding, late seeding, drought, severe grasshopper infestation, early frost and, now, snow. On top of all this we have the grain handlers' strike. The present strike will cost prairie farmers at least $10 million in demurrage charges, an unknown amount in penalties under our contracts with importing countries, and we will suffer loss of prestige and will lose our reputation for reliability as an exporter of grain. These factors will affect our grain sales for many years to come.
The Globe and Mail "Report on Business" of Friday, October 4, 1974, says the following about the grain handling situation:
Japan has been forced to buy spot cargoes of wheat at a premium from the United States because of the six-week old grain handlers' strike in Vancouver, according to the Canadian Wheat Board.
The board said yesterday that the amounts of wheat Japan was forced to buy amounted to 'hundreds of thousands of tons.'
The grain handlers' strike would have caused even more damage to Canada's reputation as a reliable exporter but for the fact there is so little available grain in the world that importers have had to stick with this country.
It will take, even under the best of circumstances, more than the balance of the year for the board to catch up with its shipping program once the strike is settled.
We cannot blame the government for the vagaries of the weather or of mother nature, but we can blame it for having brought on the strike and for failure to bring it to a quick end. I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) and compliment him on his capability and confidence. He has been well trained, possibly because he once worked for the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. He suggested that the official opposition is not concerned about settlement of the strike and said that we are using delaying tactics. He reminded me of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), who in the last session, during third reading debate on the crop insurance bill, said the opposition had deliberately delayed passage of the bill. Actually, we had asked the government often to bring it forward and said we would pass it and put up only one speaker.
Here the government is dragging red herrings across our path. When it is backed into a corner and is embarrassed, such are the tactics it uses. Sometimes they work, but not all the time. I am sure that on this occasion the farmers of western Canada will not be fooled.
October 8, 1974

I will not waste time examining the facts and the sequence of events leading up to the strike, because other spokesmen have covered them. It is sufficient to say that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) supported the minister in charge of the Wheat Board and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), who had told the grain companies to settle or the government would legislate on the basis of the Perry report, the collective bargaining process ceased and the strike became inevitable. I was interested in listening to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bas-ford) who is as skilful as other members of his party in wriggling out of embarrassing situations by making accusations.

speechtext:
Right. He quoted from the Vancouver Sun the remarks of an opposition member in Vancouver which he felt would embarrass the opposition. When called upon by members on this side to quote the balance of the news report, he ignored them. He was quick to give the impression that the opposition was in no rush to see the strike settled. I wonder whether he consulted his cohorts, the Minister of Labour and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, and saw the correspondence they had received from opposition members and members of the public.
On August 29 I wrote to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. I insisted upon the immediate calling of parliament in order that the matter could be fully debated and resolved. I did not state that I would support the legislation. With the government having stated its policy and being in a majority position, I was fully aware that any legislation presented would be passed. However, I do want the matter fully debated and resolved.
Had parliament been recalled at that time, the matter would have been resolved quickly. Millions of dollars would have been saved. It was some five weeks ago that I and other members asked that parliament be recalled. Apparently, the matter was not urgent at that time. Parliament has now been convened. After ten days of sitting, the bill has been presented. The opposition should have the opportunity of debating it for a day and a half. However, the matter has now become urgent. We are being accused of irresponsibility because we want more than one speaker to take part in this debate. Surely the opposition has some responsibility to the public to bring forth the facts and debate the matter so that the public can know what is taking place in this country.
I understand that the steering committee met yesterday. Because of the majority of government members, it was agreed that no one other than the minister and members of the Department of Labour would be called as witnesses before this standing committee. Surely members of the committee are entitled to an opportunity to have witnesses called from labour and from the government. Only in that way can the facts in dispute be brought before the public.
I have examined the Perry report. It is interesting to note the following statement in the preamble:
Grain Handlers' Strike
Given the circumstances, the recommendations which follow can hardly be expected to do more than indicate a series of intermediate changes with which both parties may be able to associate themselves as they try to conclude a settlement in a difficult year.
I read that paragraph to mean that the report was simply a basis upon which the parties should further negotiate. This is what was intended. I understand the report recommends a higher settlement than that asked for by the union. It includes many side benefits that were not even asked for. Yet the government seized on the report and made it the basis upon which they are legislating an end to this strike. It appears the government is not too clear on what is meant by the Perry report. There is a provision in clause 7 of the bill for the appointment of a referee to interpret the provisions of the Perry report if there is any dispute. Let us hope the referee appointed will be more skilful and fair than the referee who officiated in the U.S.S.R.-Canada hockey game last Sunday.
With regard to the wage increases recommended in the Perry report, there are many conflicting arguments as to the percentage increase. In his remarks last evening, the minister in charge of the Wheat Board denied that the increase was 61 per cent. He was asked several times by members on this side to give the correct figure, and he refused to answer. I should say, he parried the question with the skill of a good politician who does not know the answer or is not prepared to give it because it might embarrass him. Surely the Canadian people are entitled to know that figure.
In my view, the minister's attitude can only mean that the figure of 61 per cent is close to being correct. If this is so, in my opinion a settlement of 61 per cent will become the basis for settling future labour disputes. Certainly, other unions will be justified in asking for a settlement of this magnitude. The Prime Minister suggested this settlement really will not provide a base line. He said the present situation is unique. I disagree. If settlements of this magnitude become common, it will mean acceleration of the present rate of inflation and will lead to economic disaster in Canada.
It is interesting to note that employees of government elevators in Moose Jaw, Prince George and other areas have been for some time negotiating a settlement with the federal government. These people carry out duties similar to those of the grain handlers in Vancouver. Their base wage is lower than the Vancouver grain handlers at the present time, yet the government has seen fit to offer the employees of these government elevators an increase of only 6 per cent. Is that treating these employees fairly?
With the majority the government has in this House, and with the support of the New Democratic Party and the Social Credit Party, there is no question that this legislation will pass. However, for the reasons I have outlined, I cannot support it. The minister said an industrial commissioner will be appointed with dispatch. In addition to that, I hope he will arrange to bring together representatives of management, labour and government to discuss ways and means of solving labour disputes without resorting to strikes. Until we have a spirit of co-operation between these two groups, labour unrest will continue at tremendous cost not only to productivity but wages to employees. If this situation continues without solution, parliament

October 8, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
will be called upon time and again to carry out a function for which it was not intended.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to participate ever so briefly in this debate, not necessarily to criticize, but to make a few suggestions that this unfortunate conflict might be settled as soon as possible, and that, in the future, the government might take steps to prevent similar conflicts as much as possible.
Mr. Speaker, the government introduced the bill under study as a result of the prolonged interruption in grain handling operations.
This problem resulted in considerable losses for the Canadian economy. I shall not enumerate them; quite a few have already been discussed.
It is thus in the interest of the Canadian people and our country that operations resume at the earliest possible date.
No one, Mr. Speaker, denies the fact that the work stoppage of the grain handlers caused distress in our society. Some of its short term effects are truly disastrous. It will also have harmful effects in the long run, the brunt of which the country will have to bear.
Far be it from me to blame the workers concerned in this conflict. On the contrary, I sincerely believe that they are the victims of a seriously affected economic system. When someone is ill, we try to give him the necessary care in order that he may get well again as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, to be convinced we only have to look around and see what is happening in the country; strikes are increasing at a frightful rate and this will not help lessen the causes of inflation from which the entire population is suffering.
The bill now under consideration is aimed at the resumption of grain handling operation on the west coast of Canada; first, through the extension of the collective agreement up to November 30, 1975 if necessary and, second, through the increase of the hourly rate up to 87 cents. In my opinion, it would perhaps be possible to study the matter more closely and to improve the hourly rate.
Thirdly, there is mention of prohibiting strikes and lockouts. It is unfortunate that we had to resort to such radical means, but I believe that the moment has come to establish some authority in this country so as to maintain law and order, for the whole country is in turmoil at the present time. We had to start somewhere.
Fourthly, I agree with the bill compelling the companies and the union to negotiate. If they wish to sit down together and consider their common problems, then this bill is of no consequence. They will have to abide by it, or else, an arbitrator will have to be designated. This is another radical situation and future legislation will have to provide for cases like this one, so that it be unnecessary to recall Parliament to settle these conflicts.
Mr. Speaker, this bill will put an end to one conflict, but it will not help prevent others.
I know that this problem is exceedingly difficult. It has to conciliate money-capital with labour-capital. I know

that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) may be blamed for having failed to act sooner or still to intervene too soon. On the contrary, I personally believe that he is the victim of an obsolete system.
We are living under a capitalist regime. It is a good formula by itself, but it has become corrupted; it is sick, as I said previously. Improvements must therefore be brought in. Either such a system will be reformed by well organized men or it will be destroyed by the others. There is no middle course! This is why I find it very important for Parliament to settle not only the present dispute in the west but also to pass legislation designed to avoid others.
Conflicts between proponents of capital and labour have been going on for many years, but it clearly strikes me that they are multiplying and that they are becoming more and more serious.
We are confronted with a vicious circle, in which the increase in the cost of living forces workers to ask for higher wages; if they do not get them, workers resort to strike action. However, wage increases partly explain the increase in production costs. They might not be the only reason for this increase, but as I have already stated, they partly explain it. The increase of production costs brings about an increase in prices. These same prices decrease the workers' purchasing power, and the whole process starts over again. Mr. Speaker, this brings to mind the picture of a dog running after its tail without ever being able to catch it. It might keep on running for a long while, but its efforts will be to no avail.
Faced with the impossibility of money-capital and labour-capital to agree through negotiation, it is the government's duty to intervene, since it must act as an arbiter in encouraging, through fair legislation, the acknowledgement of the rights both of money-capital and of labour-capital. Legislative power's right to regulate working conditions has seemed in the past to be useless, ill-timed and dangerous. One need only refer to history in order to understand in what frame of mind certain of our contemporaries have shown a measure of timorousness by legislating on these matters. However, it is on behalf of the common welfare that the state has both the right and the duty to adopt protective work legislation. This care for common welfare must be both the inspiration and the measure of intervention by the state. If this concern is ignored, we will surely go wrong.
Faced with the profound transformations which have been the lot of several of our economic sectors, and with the improved state of communications, the man in the street is better informed and is becoming ever more aware of his rights. We must rejoice in that fact. Workers in particular demand that labour-capital get a larger share of the national income. Statistics show beyond a doubt that workers have not yet obtained their part of the national income, to allow them to meet their obligations as well as the steady increase in the cost of living.
The escalator formula everybody is talking about these days may be right for certain categories of people on fixed incomes. I think this formula cannot be considered as a solution, nor will it make it possible to reach the goals sought in all cases.
October 8, 1974

When salaries increase, producers boost their prices because of higher production costs. Then, workers ask again that their salaries be geared to the increase in the cost of living. Where does it stop? This is like a pyramid but nobody knows what is at the top.
I remember that a few years ago economists who wanted to disprove the economic theories of Major Douglas, the founder of Social Credit as we know it, were saying that if that economic doctrine were implemented, it would be inflation, that the pyramid of prices and salaries would be horrible, that it would be economic chaos and that the dollar would lose a great deal of its value.
Mr. Speaker, Social Credit policies have not yet been implemented, yet we have that economic chaos foreseen by those learned economists.
I think the time has come to look for other solutions so there will be a closer cooperation between money-capital and labour-capital.
My colleague the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) in taking part in this debate on this bill, made certain suggestions to prevent further conflicts which generally speaking never benefit the workers. I have never seen workers come out of a conflict better off than before.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a suggestion to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and this government that could promote better understanding between employers and employees. I am talking about the participation of workers in businesses. Whether we like it or not, that will be the ultimate solution if we want to get the maximum out of our human and material resources for the greatest benefit of all Canadians.
Participation of workers in the company, this is how we could call this new policy. However, the formula of worker participation in company profits must not overshadow the fact that there must also be participation of the workers in the development of Canadian companies. Not only do we have rights in our society, but we also have duties that we must accept if there is to be some order. And I insist on the fact that there must be development, not only through the investment of labour-capital, which in my opinion, is the most important aspect, but also through the investment of money-capital when profits allow it, or by any other means.
Mr. Speaker, the international congress of participation in profits which was held in France in 1889 defined participation in profits as follows: a voluntary agreement under which the employee receives a predetermined part of the profits.
Another method has also been suggested according to which an employer makes available to his regular employees, in addition to their ordinary wages, immediate or deferred payments based on company profits.
Another method could also be advanced to increase production and reduce costs. This involves the human cooperation brought about by the direct participation of employees who, in addition to their regular wages, benefit from company results measured in profits, which means that the more effective the company is, the more significant its results. But the worker could share in this effectiveness in some financial capacity.
Grain Handlers' Strike
This system of worker participation in the company was suggested in France around 1850, and the company that had the good idea of allowing its employees to participate in its profits never had any conflicts in its plants. This company still operates and has more than 1,000 employees. This has not stopped its development. On the contrary, it has developed even more.
Participation is now a human right. Every man must be co-author, co-responsible and co-beneficiary as far as the work of the company is concerned. Everybody has a right and a duty to participate. In this sense, the problem of participation must be set in terms of the rights of those concerned rather than in terms of the duties of management. Participation must go as far as the transformation of the business structures. These new structures must allow a continuing dialogue, not one that takes place every 18 or 24 months.
But these new structures must not encompass a sharing of authority. On the contrary, the managers must always retain the responsibilities of direction. We might discuss endlessly whether such a participation is a right of the workers but in any case, most business managers have always been more concerned with their interests than their responsibilities. It is high time they should be reminded of their duties.
Nowadays, there is no more room for mistakes in assessing workers mentality. The systematic denial of participation in a certain management of the business is the main reason which I think makes unions and workers tend to socialism and its extreme form, communism. Their social responsibilities are extremely important, but if they are not carried, we are heading for a period of violence and restlessness.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I think it was relevant to ponder over this problem and make the suggestions I have presented and which I will repeat to conclude my remarks.
In order to reach that goal, the government will necessarily have to bring amendments to the fiscal legislation so as to ensure tax benefits to workers who will participate financially in the company besides participating through their work. It does not behove me to find the formula that would be suitable. I am making that suggestion and I am convinced that whenever there are benefits there are inevitably people who are interested. Such changes would entail certain tax benefits for companies and that goes for employers as well as workers.
We must also be convinced that the government should make it its duty to ensure all members of our society a reasonable participation in the production of wealth so they may all secure a sufficient living income.
That is why I am saying again today that work is an instrument given by the Creator to process in a detailed form what he put in bulk on this earth and that work will always remain an extremely valuable instrument. We must strive all together to bring the notion of work into currency again in the mind of our people who are going through difficult times.
Finally, the formula of the annual minimum guaranteed income advocated by the Social Credit party of Canada would greatly contribute to the solution of those problems, as it would enable workers to get a larger income without
222

October 8, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
that part of the income affecting prices. That way, we would avoid runaway inflation.
I am more convinced than ever, Mr. Speaker, that the time has come for this government to listen attentively to Major Douglas' suggestions and ideas instead of rejecting them outright as unpractical.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that really valuable suggestions were made during this debate and that the government, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and his advisers should read over again the speeches made during this debate in order to lay down such policies that we may hope in the future that the Canadian people will not have to put up with disputes of that kind but on the contrary, that there would be an agreement between labour-capital and money-capital and that it would be beneficial to everyone.
