subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate being allowed to make a few comments

during this debate since I too represent a constituency in which farming plays a very vital role, namely, the northwestern portion of the Peace River country. Before getting to my general remarks I should like to respond to a few comments by some of my colleagues earlier, particularly those of the minister responsible for the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang). From what he said last night he seems to think the Conservatives have found a new ally in their attempt to place the burden of inflation on the backs of the workers, and that it would be our attempt to blame the government for this.
The minister comes from a farming community, and I dare say that he has at one time worked on a farm. I wonder if he does not consider the farmers of this country to be working people. The farmers are the people who will ultimately have to pay the cost and suffer the consequences of the imposition of this bill on the grain handling companies in Vancouver.
Last night the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bas-ford) concentrated on embarrassing a few of my newer colleagues. He was challenged by members in Vancouver to comment on this strike when it became apparent. Certainly we said that parliament should be recalled after the government intervened and told grain companies that parliament would settle the strike.
It was quite obvious to any thinking person in Canada that there would be no settlement of this strike until parliament intervened. Why should the grain companies in Vancouver take the responsibility for this settlement and its consequences? The minister said that the bargaining process had broken down so the government had to intervene. I suggest the bargaining process broke down because of the suggested intervention by parliament.
The minister also said, and I hope I misunderstood or am misinterpreting him, that this bill is similar to bills dealing with other disputes in the past. This bill is not the same, because last year when we settled the railway workers' strike we left a position for bargaining in the provisions of the bill. We established a floor position from which to bargain. This bill does not provide any such thing but rather imposes a settlement, and appoints a referee to see that it is implemented.
The minister said that in 1973, because of a minority position, we had to establish a position from which to bargain, but that this is not necessary today. That statement worries me no end. I wonder if we are now all alone like a voice in the wilderness, with the government assuming its power of the July 8 mandate. I hope that is not the case.
A former leader of the NDP, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), said he felt it his responsibility to intervene on behalf of the prairie farmers. Everyone knows that the prairie farmers are against this settlement since it is they who will have to pay the bill. I suggest he is not intervening on behalf of the farmers but is intervening on behalf of a principle we will all have to live with, not just in respect of the grain industry but in respect of any other labour settlement in which we become involved in the future.
My comments will be of a general nature as I have no intention to attempt to take sides in this dispute between
October 8, 1974

the grain companies and the union. I would be reluctant to intervene at all were it not for the fact that there are three parties to this unfortunate situation, the third party being the government.
It is the government that cites this bill as something to settle all the problems relating to grain handling on the west coast, totally ignoring the fact that there are grain handling facilities in Victoria and in Prince Rupert. The difference between the grain handling facilities in Vancouver and those in Prince Rupert is that those in Prince Rupert are owned and operated by the federal government.
This government wants to impose this settlement on the grain handling companies in Vancouver, and this is the government that neglected shipping potential of 30 millions bushels this summer out of the port of Prince Rupert. We have a new member in the House from Prince Rupert representing the fine constituency of Skeena. I note that she is in the House. Knowing that she is very concerned about this serious problem I hope she will listen to what I have to say.
In June 1974, the elevators in Prince Rupert were plugged. There were 300 rail cars destined for Prince Rupert that could not be unloaded because there were no ships. All the ships were in Vancouver Harbour incurring $5,000 to $7,000 per day in demurrage.
Some 2,000 cars were processed in April and May of 1973 through the port of Prince Rupert. In September of the same year there was no movement in that port. This resulted in the layoff of all the trained people who normally handled grain. In December we decided that Prince Rupert port should play an important part in the movement of grain in western Canada, and two ships were put on to handle grain out of Prince Rupert. A large training program was launched, involving a number of people who, incidentally, are federal employees and for that reason are likely classified as second-class citizens. At least no one talks about them. The whole program was scrapped and these people were laid off in January, presumably because we did not want to get into competition with private enterprise in Vancouver. I do not know what the reason was, but that was the situation.
The responsible minister is not in the House and I am sure the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) is not aware of the potential role people might play in other areas on the west coast. I hope the new hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnola) will study the situation, and use her influence and charm to persuade some of her colleagues in the front benches that the port of Prince Rupert can play a much greater role in the future, with the result that some of these problems might be avoided.
I wish to make some comments about Canada's labour situation in general and the involvement of government in labour problems. Normally I divide Canada's labour force into three categories. The first is what I call an elite group. The number in this group is quite small. I would estimate it represents about 15 per cent of Canada's labour force. It does not necessarily involve the highest wages and fringe benefits in Canada, nor do members of this group pride
Grain Handlers' Strike
themselves on having the best working conditions. On the contrary.
Even though these people compose the elite group, they are often at the bottom of the scale in respect of all categories. I call this the elite group because the services of these people are indispensable not only to the employers but also to our country. These are the people who perform essential public services in Canada. They are key people. By virtue of their trades they enjoy prestige. Their disputes, relations, pensions and conditions of work can be and often are settled by Parliament.
Now, one would assume that that category should be far ahead of all others having this access to the highest tribunal in the country. The reason this is not so, however, must be attributed to the fact that our government really has not been able adequately to solve any problem in which it interfered in recent times. I do not have the time to comment at length on some of the settlements in which we have been involved in recent times.
The second group consists of about 25 per cent of Canada's labour force. These people, like their colleagues from the elite group, are organized by a variety of unions through which they compete for and have achieved the country's highest wages, fringe benefits, and most advantageous working conditions. They are mainly employed by the private sector of industry. The reason for the prosperity of this group is twofold. First, these people enjoy a status called "citizens plus", which means that while they have all the protection of Parliament through the Canada Labour Act, they are responsible to no one, and Parliament will not rule them back to work.
Second, they are bargaining with a sector of our corporate system which, by virtue of conglomerate, and monopolistic business practices can of course afford better than any other sector of our business community to respond positively to the demands placed upon them by their work force.
The third group is comprised of 60 per cent of our work force. It does not enjoy the benefit nor the protection of Parliament or union and its members' standard of living reflects the horrible situation in which these people find themselves. Sure, Mr. Speaker, we have introduced a minimum wage act. But, even with that protection, in most cases they earn less than the poor who are already on the welfare rolls. Most provinces have also passed legislation designed to protect all of our work force, such as workmen's compensation, statutory holidays and so on.
However, Mr. Speaker, when it really comes down to bare facts, we know that there are only a privileged few who divide among themselves the country's prosperity. The situation in which we end up is such that one third of our work force enjoys two thirds of the benefits and income. Why this is so is not hard to understand. Unions, often controlled from outside our country, have become more conscious of building large and monstrous pension funds and competing with the large corporations for efficiency in operation. No attempt is made to enlarge their membership to include all of Canada's work force in their mandate.
Unions have, in fact, admitted that they are reluctant to extend their activities into so-called unproductive areas,

October 8, 1974

or areas where the economy is unable to absorb or fill demands placed on it by the unions. Meanwhile there is really no question that Parliament and legislators have submitted to pressures from these unions, and have established them with powers over their membership which are in serious conflict with the Canadian Bill of Rights, and which restrict the freedom of the individual.
The most obvious example of that is, of course, the fact that we are making it a condition of employment in unionized industries to show proof of membership in a union. Thus, if a man falls out with his union, he does not work. This is particularly unrealistic since governments have ruled out competition among various unions through certification. A perfect example of that, of course, is the Public Service Alliance, and the problem we had with the firefighters last year who were not in difficulty with their employer since the employer wanted to resolve the difficulty, but whose real legal strike was with the union with which they were in conflict and not the employer.
Once a union has achieved certification in any one business or industry, it rules supremely over its membership. For that reason, it is more often the rule than the exception that decisions taken by the unions do not reflect the wishes of the membership at large. Even if we disregard this obvious discrepancy in our democratic process, it still remains a fact that our economy does not have sufficient resources to equalize the opportunity, or even to narrow the gap between the organized and the unorganized worker.
The double standard which therefore exists for Canadians has established two categories of poor as well, namely, the working poor and the unemployed poor. To compound the situation, we only measure the workmans' life standard by his disposable income. I suppose we accept that if a person's disposable income is already below the poverty line he also cannot be expected to place any demands on fringe benefits such as working conditions, holidays and overtime pay. The fact is that unless any one of the unorganized two-thirds majority can rely on the charity of his employer, he is a second class citizen.
The employer of this segment of our labour force is the small businessman or secondary industry, whose contribution to our prosperity is never recognized. The irony is that the corporate sector of our system, backed by conglomerate and monopolistic positions, is setting a pace and a standard which are impossible to achieve by the business community which still subscribes and subjects itself to the rules of free enterprise and individual freedom and initiative. The irony also is that the corporate sector has joined forces with unions, thus protecting its own interests as well.
I am beginning to question whether it is not high time for us to follow the lead of other industrialized countries, with a lot less problems in this area, in insisting that our country's opportunities and achievements are adequately distributed. Is it not time, Mr. Speaker, to insist that at least the fringe benefits for a day's work in our country are the same, regardless of the field of endeavour in which a working person might be, and of whether he or she is protected by the political muscle of an union? There is, of course, and there always will be the need for labour unions, but let them collectively bargain with the govern-

ment for a greater share of the country's wealth not just for their own members but for all Canadians.
It has never been fair to say that excessive labour demands are solely responsible for the high rate of inflation in Canada but if we establish a precedent, as we seem about to be doing in the grain handlers' dispute in Vancouver, whereby legislation might impose a settlement on this very vital sector of our community which is even in excess of union demands, we are setting a very dangerous precedent, particularly at a time when the prime producers of grain and other agricultural commodities should concentrate their efforts and resources on expansion and improved efficiency of their operations.
Mr. Speaker, the companies involved in the dispute have never refused to bargain, but they have refused to negotiate under conditions imposed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang). They have taken a position against the dictatorial attitude of the government, for which I cannot blame them. The minister, after all, has openly blackmailed the companies. He said, "You settle, or parliament will legislate your settlement". The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) confirmed later in a telegram to the companies that the two ministers indeed spoke for the government. I have a copy of the telegram, Mr. Speaker, and this is what the Prime Minister said:
When Mr. Munro and Mr. Lang advised that the Perry recommendations would be legislated if no settlement was reached prior to reassembly of parliament, I can assure you they were speaking for the government.
These are indeed strange circumstances for the process of collective bargaining, Mr. Speaker. In my opinion, this does not create a climate for responsible and intelligent industrial relations proceedings. The companies will make the government carry out its threat and the government will of course have no alternative to living up to its commitment to the union, using their comfortable majority position in the House of Commons to impose a settlement. There will not be, of course, any defiance of the law as a result of this settlement once it is passed. This is normally the case when parliament or a legislature imposes settlement on a union. But, Mr. Speaker, I for one place responsibility for the consequences, not only of this settlement but the impact it will have on future negotiations, squarely on the shoulders of this government.
Let us leave to the unions only the bargaining for wages and salaries which must obviously differ in various professions and trades. But, as in the case of countries where the industrial relations process has advanced with the times, it should be the union's prime concern to assure for its members a greater degree of job security and to demand from its membership a much higher level of professional conduct and work ethics, as well as a more responsible attitude toward the economic welfare of the country as a whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not go so far as to say it is a pleasure to take part in the debate on this legislation, but it seems that we must debate it because of the bumbling of three senior cabinet ministers. Last night the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) pleaded with us in an effort to get himself and other ministers off the hook. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the official opposition has no intention of letting them off the hook. They were bleeding yesterday, and they need to bleed a bit more because of the unforgivable sin they have committed by their actions in this regard. They should not have participated at all. In order to protect their own interests and to get past the election, they used the Canada Labour Code, and yesterday had the audacity to tell us that we must put this legislation through quickly, although the election is three months past. Madam Speaker, this case will be known as the big bungle of 1974 created by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, backed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
We are not just dealing with 550 people, but with the economy of the whole country. I am sure every Canadian recognizes that the economic pie is only so large and can only be cut into so many pieces. If any one segment of the economy takes too much of the pie, it is taking something that belongs to others. This is exactly what we are dealing with in this legislation. One segment of the economy is seizing an opportunity that was handed to them on a platter prior to an election. This is very significant and I think it should be pointed out. The Canadian public is entitled to ask if there was a sell-out.
Last night the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, replying to comments of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin), said:
Let me say that I am happy to note that a few members who said nasty things about me in the previous parliament and who came from Saskatchewan are not here to join their colleague. I was interested to listen to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, because he was speaking in his last term as member of parliament. We have a short list and he is at the top.
Did the government have a list prior to the election, Madam Speaker? Do they expect Canadian grain producers to pay their bill for the support they got in defeating 15 members of the New Democratic Party? Why would the minister make a statement like that if it has no basis in fact? Does this mean that in the next election 15 more NDP members will disappear?

speechtext:
The question we have to ask is, what will this decision do to the economy of Canada? I suppose if any one of us was a member of the union involved, and had the opportunity of taking advantage of the presumptuous comment made by the minister, we would all jump on the bandwagon. Yet, what about the rest of the economy? What about the 1,500 grain handlers on the Great Lakes? Are they to get 61 per cent also?
Perhaps we should clarify the figures. There is some discrepancy as to the percentages used. Some say the grain handlers will get 48 per cent, some say 61 per cent. Why has this discrepancy arisen? The reason is that no one really knows what the consumer price index will be in future, and the 61 per cent is based on a 1 per cent rise in inflation per month. Let me point out that the grain companies are owned 80 per cent by the grain producers of western Canada. I hope the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) remembers this: he was elected by grain producers and sent here to look after their well-being, not to preserve the big, red Liberal machine.
We have to consider what can happen to the economy. What about the grain inspectors? If they do not work, they could stop grain shipments just as effectively as the grain handlers-and they are getting less. What about elevator operators? The 3,500 elevator operators across the country are getting 40 cents an hour less than the grain handlers, at the present rates. What will the government do with its own employees? I am not merely talking about grain inspectors. For instance, in my constituency it is interesting to consider wages paid by the provincial and federal governments for similar work. Plumbers employed provincially receive $1,262 per month; those employed federally receive $916. The yearly spread is over $4,000.
Provincial electricians are paid $1,263 a month; federal electricians, $964, which comes to a difference of about $4,000 per annum. Provincially employed carpenters receive $1,123; if federally employed, $778. Again, the difference is $4,000. Painters, if employed provincially, are paid $1,018; if employed federally, $722. Trade help is paid $792 provincially, and $573 federally. Labourers are paid $724 by the province, and $509 by the federal government. Some of these people are paid about $6,000 a year, on which the federal government says they must subsist. Grain handlers are not paid $6,000. Today they are paid salaries ranging from $16,000 to $18,000 a year. These are wages that grain producers must pay.

October 8, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
When commenting during the throne speech debate on his intention to reform parliamentary rules and procedures, the Prime Minister said this was necessary to expedite House of Commons business. He also said it is time for Canada to move beyond the kindergarten stage. Surely those comments apply to the situation now facing parliament. Today we are spending time in settling an issue resulting from irresponsible action by two cabinet ministers. They will suffer more when this bill goes to committee because we shall ask them embarrassing questions and they will have to answer for their actions.
In my opinion, before we in this House are urged to amend the rules and enable the government to rush its legislation through following four months of inactivity, top priority should be given to having the ministers concerned act with maturity instead of like kindergarten pupils. I might add that if all cabinet members faced up to their responsibilities and obeyed parliamentary rules, our time would not be wasted.
If this government had not interfered in the negotiations between the grain handlers and the grain companies, if it had not done so through the bumbling, inept actions of the two ministers previously mentioned, negotiations could have continued and I feel sure a settlement would have been reached weeks ago. Immediately those ministers came out in support of the recommendations of the Perry report, further collective bargaining became futile and the dispute ground to a standstill. We are all aware now, if we were not before, what a few words uttered without forethought by irresponsible persons in authority can cost this country, our economy and our relations with our foreign customers for grain. This episode, as it unfolded, resembled a Grimm's fairy tale which is suitable for performance on a stage. Unfortunately, it really happened, with the result that every Canadian has suffered.
Last November, when the collective agreement between the grain handlers and the terminal operators at Vancouver expired, management offered an increase of 80 cents per hour for a one-year agreement. Conciliation efforts failed, and in February the Minister of Labour appointed Dr. Perry as commissioner. On May 24, during the election campaign, the Minister of Labour announced that the government had taken action by order in council, under section 181 of the Canada Labour Code, to make a strike or lock-out illegal until August 8, one month following election day. On May 24 he also said at a Vancouver news conference:
The government will introduce legislation to approve contract recommendations by conciliator Dr. Perry as a binding collective agreement on the two parties.
On what advice or consideration was such a cowardly step based? I hope hon. members opposite recognize the importance of the situation with which we are dealing. On July 18 the Minister of Labour reaffirmed the government's decision to force settlement terms upon the grain companies. The minister responsible for the Wheat Board urged producers to exert pressure on their own organizations in order that the inflationary conciliation recommendation would be accepted. What right did he have to do that? A telegram sent by the two ministers to the grain companies on August 23 reads in part:
We have made it quite clear, as has the Prime Minister, that the

government will legislate the recommendations of Dr. Perry if necessary.
Of course, that position met resistance. Why? Because the grain companies are owned by the producers and they backed the companies up to the hilt. Ninety per cent of them supported the companies. What else could they do? What else could the companies do, if they were to discharge their responsibility to those they served? Clearly, the three members of the government previously referred to have put the government into an intolerable position. Let me put on record letters which the companies have received from farmers. I quote a letter from Cupar, Saskatchewan:
Do I, as a grain farmer, also get a 61 per cent increase in the price of my products? In two years time can I negotiate as a body for another 60 per cent increase? ... I agree that when the cost of living increases 10 per cent, so should everything else-not 60 per cent. I, as a farmer, am finally able to get my head a little above water. If price and wages increase at the same rate, that water is going to get... deep again. Keep up the good work.
From Pipestone, Manitoba, came this letter:
Let the government force the issue, so as to let the people of Canada see more clearly what is happening to inflation and the cause of it. Thanks.
Next is a letter from Brandon, Manitoba:
The Perry report recommendations are excessive to the extreme. Congratulations on your stand re this issue. The membership of UGG are solidly behind you.
Next comes a letter from Myrtle, Manitoba:
Request government to take immediate action. If the government is as concerned about western agriculture as they say they are, they will move ... fast.
Next is a letter from Boissevain, Manitoba:
If governments continue to allow ... high increases to unions, private enterprise will have to follow. If they feel food is at a high price now, it will have to increase with the wages. Somebody must take a stand some time.
Next I quote part of a letter sent from Yorkton, Saskatchewan:
Aside from the reaction of other labour sectors, there could be a repercussion in our own company, particularly among elevator managers.
These employees, as I said previously, are receiving 40 cents an hour less than grain handlers. I want to impress on this House that grain producers, on average, are getting 50 per cent less than this agreement will provide for grain handlers. We are dealing with a very touchy situation. We must recognize that the price of machinery for grain producers increased between 25 and 30 per cent the last year. The cost of repairs increased 30 per cent. Fertilizer went from $106 to $168 a ton, an increase of 59 per cent. Increases of this magnitude are apparent throughout the system. There is no way in which producers can stay in business if they continually have to face this type of inflation from every direction. They will lose their incentive, and if that happens we will be in a very sorry state indeed. We will have done a great disservice to the economy of this country.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this bill has been debated exhaustively and there are very few things that can still be said. We are debating a settlement
October 8, 1974

forced upon the grain co-operatives by the government. It is the end of a long period in which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) have bungled the situation. That is what necessitated this action.
There are many matters to be considered. First, when does a conciliation report by a labour relations officer, as opposed to an arbitration report, become absolutely necessary? It should be pointed out that a conciliation report is a basis upon which to negotiate further. The conciliator does not expect all his suggestions to be accepted. There is still room for negotiation. However, the ministers have made it plain that they regard the conciliation report as an arbitration report to be forced on the grain co-operatives.
This piece of legislation will deal with the problem of approximately 550 grain handlers, against the four major grain companies, the Alberta Wheat Pool, the Pacific Elevator Company, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, United Grain Growers Limited, and a very small private company, Burrard Terminals. These companies represent 175,000 permit holders. Almost all permit holders in western Canada have a share in one of these co-operatives. They represent one million people who live on the farm. These people have a direct interest in this problem and how much a settlement will cost. It is the farmers who will have to pay the cost of the settlement. It is their grain co-operatives, not private grain companies, who are negotiating on their behalf.
We have heard a great deal about demurrage charges. Some thought these would be paid by the federal treasury. They will come out of the final amount the farmer will receive. The cost of the settlement will lessen the amount of money that will eventually be returned to the producer. Therefore, the million people on the farms have a right to have their companies put forward their case so that the cost of settling will be as low as possible. The settlement should not be exorbitant. It is sometimes forgotten that these grain companies are owned by upward of one million people on the prairies.
Prairie grain growers live in a land-locked area. To the west, he must traverse the Rocky Mountains to the seaport; to the east, the Laurentians and the Great Lakes to reach the port of Montreal and ocean vessels. In all this transportation, the railways and shipping companies have a monopoly. Dozens of groups are involved in the transportation of grain. It is highly vulnerable. There is a widespread effect of stoppage by any one relatively small group of employees. This makes the efficient movement of grain a very hazardous operation. The prairie farmer sells on the world market. What he receives is that price, minus the difference between what the various groups charge for handling and transportation of the grain. With the upcoming problems, this will not be the last grain stoppage. As soon as this settlement is reached, another will take its place.
It is particularly bad that the government decided on a settlement of 60 per cent, considerably in excess of that asked by the union. That makes the whole exercise very disturbing. The action of the Minister of Labour and the minister in charge of the wheat board ruled out any settlement that was not enforced by parliament. The Minister of Labour did not seek the approval of the grain
Grain Handlers' Strike
companies and co-operatives in the appointment of Dr. Perry to write a conciliation report. In this way he was inviting trouble. It is not evident that Dr. Perry had any special knowledge of the grain handling business. He looked upon this as a labour problem to be settled. The eventual buyer of the grain would pay for it. Not only did he give more than that asked by the union, but he threw in two or three doubtful settlements that have been written into the legislation.
Dr. Perry recommended a wage increase of $1.52 over two years. I think that was reasonable. I know the grain co-operatives, the Alberta pool, the Saskatchewan pool, the United Grain Growers and the farmers they represent expected and were prepared to pay an increase. The government could well have requested the grain workers to go back to work, and management to again open the terminals at the wage increase of $1.52 an hour. Other aspects of this settlement could have been dealt with at a later date. In fact, the Minister of Labour said he had proposed to the grain co-operatives changes in the cost of living clause and of the pension plan. This, he says, would have considerably reduced the cost. However, he has never made public these changes, and they are disputed by the companies.
I think Dr. Perry's recommendation, that a cost of living clause be built into this plan, is highly dangerous. Surely the recommended $1.52 an hour takes into account the projected cost of living for the next two years. All wage increases, demands and agreements take into account the cost of living increase. In pensions, this is done by indexing. Family allowances, welfare payments and old age pensions are protected by a cost of living index. I think that is good for those who are unable to bargain. However, must there be a cost of living clause in every wage agreement? This implies that there should be a cost of living adjustment for the farmer in the production of his milk or cream, as well as for the automobile manufacturer and others. If we write this cost of living clause into all wage agreements, we will be inviting trouble. It may be all right for those who cannot fend for themselves, but for other parts of the economy it is a very bad practice.
It has been well said that much of the prosperity of the last 25 years has been based on the erosion of savings, but with the value of money being eroded, those responsible for making savings eventually found that they did not receive the value of what they had saved. Also, the importance of private pension plans seems to be declining and their future is extremely doubtful.
I notice that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) is in his place. He introduced amendments to the Canada Pension Plan which did not pass. I should like to ask him when is he bringing another bill forward, and whether he expects it to contain a clause dealing with the question of religious sects?
I think we are reaching the stage at which the old age pension and the Canada pension are so basic that private pension plans will become redundant. I do not believe they should be encouraged. This, of course, is a debatable proposition and I do not intend to expand on it now. Nevertheless, I think we ought to look charily at new private pension programs. Incidentally, I am informed

October 8, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
that the grain handlers did have a private pension plan some years ago but that they threw it out, for reasons with which I am not familiar. Eventually all private pension plans will need to be dovetailed into the Canada Pension Plan.
This settlement is highly inflationary and it is bound to be followed by further costly settlements throughout the industry. We can expect prolonged stoppages in the movement of grain. It should be realized that the more money it costs to move and transport our grain, the less the farmer eventually receives, and this, in turn, discourages production. Nor is it generally realized how much farm costs have been increasing. A pail of Avidex which only this spring cost $59 is now $83.
During this dispute it has been suggested by many that the Vancouver terminals are poorly managed and inefficiently operated. The union leader, to his credit, has spoken convincingly about his intense desire to improve productivity and management at the Vancouver terminal. He wishes to see this done, in his own words, "far beyond previous levels in the interest of the western grain farmer". What are the facts?
In May, June and July of last year unloadings at Vancouver averaged 609 cars a day. The corresponding figure for this year is 393 cars a day with a plentiful supply of cars on hand. What happened to the desire to unload cars rapidly? No matter how much renovation is carried out, if the workers are unwilling to work, or if management is unwilling to manage, one cannot expect much efficiency. How does reduction of productivity by more than one-third of demonstrated ability tie in with Mr. Kanes' dedication to attaining high standards of efficiency?
Dr. Perry, the Minister of Labour, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) among others, have stressed the need for parity of income with that of longshoremen performing similar tasks to members of local 333 on the same waterfront. This is put forward as justification for the costly settlement recommended. However, as has been pointed out in this debate, the argument loses impact in the light of the offer made by the negotiating committee of the Treasury Board to Vancouver grain inspectors working for the Canadian Grain Commission.
The inspectors found the offer of a 6 per cent wage increase over 18 months, with a further 5Vi per cent over the following 12 months, entirely unacceptable, and in a letter to the Prime Minister they drew attention to his statement that parity ought to exist between the pay of grain handlers and longshoremen.
Under the Perry report, Vancouver grain handlers would get a basic rate of $6.44. The basic rate for grain inspectors is only $4.33. I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that inspector status is achieved only after years of study and the passing of rigorous examinations. After all, the inspectors are the men upon whose judgment the reputation of the Canadian grain grading system depends. It is in on their authority that the export certificate is issued. In these circumstances we must accept it as a fact that the grain inspectors are almost certain to go off the job once this strike is settled.
Moreover, I believe we must get the relationship between grain handlers and longshore workers into a more

reasonable perspective. A grain handler, at least if he belongs to what I understand is called the first shift, is assured of steady work. A longshoreman may go to his union hiring hall in the morning, but he is not sure of finding work that day. So the longshoreman is paid on the basis that on many days of the year there will be no work available for him. To compare longshoremen with grain handlers is like comparing longshoremen with miners or Members of Parliament.
It has been suggested that this dispute should be settled at any cost without much discussion. This view is put forward partly on the ground that Canada's reputation as a reliably consistent supplier is being damaged. I understand that at one time Japan used to buy all her wheat from Canada, but after supplies had been interrupted due to a strike by longshoremen at Vancouver, orders from then on had to be shared with the United States and Australia. Thus, to say the present stoppage is particularly damaging does not sound to me like a really good argument.
Last year we had a six weeks railway strike. Last winter the prairies experienced the most severe snowfall that most of us can remember. Many of the rail lines were closed. Yet if hon. members look at the statistics they will find that despite these adversities we got out all the grain we had to sell-there was very little left over. The world, of course, is very short of grain, perhaps for the first time in 25 years. News that the United States has cancelled a contract to sell wheat to Russia underlines this state of affairs. So it is likely there will be a good market for Canadian grain this year even though surpluses may arise in the years to come.
The storage of substantial quantities of Canadian grain abroad should be examined. This would help to supply our customers when our own transportation system is not functioning. Another possibility would be the movement of grain into the U.S. mid-west in modest amounts, and no doubt the American railways would be happy to transport grain, our grain, to the markets of the world. If western Canadian farmers are left at the mercy of stoppages of many different kinds, it is wise to have as many options open to us as possible.
We live in a free country and most of us want to keep it that way. The strike weapon is a legitimate means for a worker to use to ensure he gets a reasonable wage. I must say that, in my opinion, the government's handling of this whole case has not improved the possibility of good relations between unions, the farmers on the prairies, the people who own the co-operatives and the grain handling companies.
I hope that in the committee the minister will be able to tell us what offer he made to the grain companies which would lessen the cost of this settlement, and what specific cost to the companies he has worked out. There are many unanswered questions in this whole sorry affair, and perhaps our committee system will prove of value in ferreting them out.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to take the opportunity to
October 8, 1974

rise in the House, though I regret I am rising in a debate of this nature rather than on the throne speech debate, as was my first intention.
It had been thought by some people that if the government felt there was urgency to this matter it would have had a certain presence about it and brought in a settlement, or the means of arriving at a settlement, at the time it dictated the solution. However, the government has procrastinated and delayed and we now find it interrupting the throne speech debate. Once again we find parliament has been pulled into the unfortunate situation of settling a strike of great importance to this country through legislation.
The present strike is of grave importance, and it is detrimental to Canada for three reasons. One reason is that the strike affects our international relations. We cannot keep faith with countries that made commitments with us. We cannot perform in accordance with our international contracts. We cannot deliver what we have promised. Quite frankly, this is bad for Canada. It gives Canada a bad reputation in the international community, and I suggest could even jeopardize future contracts.
Secondly, this strike has disrupted, and threatens to do future damage to the grain economy upon which so much of the economy of western Canada is dependent. It has affected not only our shipments but has caused a backlog of grain deliveries, with last year's grain being held in elevators instead of being shipped to ports, leaving no room to store this year's grain in the elevators. This in turn will put the farmers and the people of western Canada to extra expense in arranging for storage upon their own lands until some room can be found at the elevators.
Thirdly, it is an unfortunate and detrimental strike because demurrage charges for ships waiting in western ports are costing farmers and others a large amount of money. Farmers are being forced to spend money on storing wheat instead of injecting it into the economy. This means that a much wider group of Canadians than simply those who are the employees of the elevator operators or grain handling companies are hurt. They are playing with dollars that they do not rightfully own. It is not their money.
For these three reasons, and for others that have been amply discussed in the debate today, this strike has hurt us and hurt our economy. Our grain industry and grain exports are both essential to Canada's economy, especially in the western provinces.
The people of my constituency, Madam Speaker, and I believe the people of Canada as a whole, are sick and tired of strikes in important essential services.

I am speaking for myself and as the representative for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton. The Minister of
Grain Handlers' Strike
National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) happens to be in the House at the present time, and it is nice to see him here although the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was crying the other day that ministers did not even have time to attend the question period. However, I see him chuckling and I guess he now has nothing else to do.
It seems to me that every year or so workers in one of our public utilities or essential services go on strike. In most cases these public utilities or essential services are monopolies, and there is a very limited choice of alternative service from a like source. These public utilities or essential services include such operations as Bell Canada, Ontario Hydro in this part of Canada, Air Canada, our post offices, ocean port facilities, grain handling facilities, our railways and suchlike.
Each time a strike or lockout takes place and one of these essential services closes, or its function is impaired, we, the public, suffer. To be sure, the companies and workers who are out of work suffer, but they have brought it upon themselves and that is their business. It becomes our business when we, the general public, are affected by the shutdown and become the pawns in a labour-management dispute. Each time one of our essential services closes down or its operation is impaired, thousands of innocent people, not involved in the dispute but working in related and dependent industries, are also put out of work. In many cases businesses suffer to the extent that they may be permanently closed down.
When the post office workers were on strike illegally last year, Dunn and Bradstreet reported numerous businesses were forced to close permanently because of a lack of cash flow. When our port facilities are shut down, our railwaymen go on strike, or our grain handlers go on strike, the whole economy suffers and the innocent public have to shoulder the burden of the comparatively few who have closed down the essential service in question. This should not be so. The political parties of this country ought to move to protect the public from the direct effects of strikes in essential services.
The party to which I belong, the Progressive Conservative party, has for some time now advocated a two-fold policy in this field. Firstly, in essential services under federal jurisdiction we would encourage collective bargaining throughout the term of a contract, not just at the end. But we would clearly indicate that we would withdraw the right to strike, and that binding arbitration would be the final step in resolving differences.
Secondly, the Progressive Conservative Party has endorsed the recommendations presented to the government in December, 1968, contained in the Woods Commission Report for the establishment of a public interest disputes commission. Such a public interest disputes commission would define which services are essential and would set up a procedure for binding arbitration.
Our country and our economy cannot afford national disruptions of our essential services which stop functioning because of a selfish view, all of which penalizes the public at large.
Unfortunately parliament today is again being used as a court of final resort. We are put in the position of the final
230

October 8, 1974

arbiter, and this should not be the case. In this way we are derogating the responsibilities of parliament which should be to pass impartially laws for all Canadians to follow.
When parliament is drawn into a dispute involving strikes it ends up taking sides. By becoming involved, parliament encourages other parties not to negotiate in good faith. We may be encouraging other parties who are at this time at the bargaining table to break off negotiations, to protract negotiations, or to cause such a disruption that their case will finally be forced before parliament. If this were to become the norm, parliament could ultimately end up carrying on labour negotiations for the whole session.
Another unfortunate aspect of these matters coming before parliament is that politicians usually give in to politically expedient decisions. Frequently, if not always, when parliament becomes involved a settlement is inflationary. The best example of this, and the one which has been frequently cited as the cornerstone from which our economic difficulties have stemmed, especially in management-union relations, is the dispute and strike of the Montreal port workers in 1966, when a settlement was reached by the government of Mr. Pearson. The government was then under the gun because unless there was a settlement Expo '67 could not take place. Since that time we have not had evidence of negotiations taking place honestly in good faith. We have not had evidence that the demand for intervention has lessened, but we have seen a general trend toward inflationary settlements.
Today we are talking about a settlement referred to as being in the nature of 48 per cent to 61 per cent. The government brought on this unfortunate situation by its intervention. It did not let the bargaining process complete its normal course, and it did not use the legislation it had on hand under the labour code. Perhaps through coercion it would have persuaded the parties to get together, but instead it blandly came out and endorsed the Perry report.
As a result there was no need to negotiate further. The unions already felt they had what they wanted. What sense was there for the pools to negotiate? The case had already been settled. In effect the government had settled this strike, but it forgot one main ingredient. It forgot in August to bring forward a means of implementing the settlement it had dictated.
Why did the government waste time once it had confirmed the Perry report? Why did it wait an additional six weeks before bringing this matter before the House of Commons? The government had already indicated its intention to place the matter before parliament for legislative action. I suggest it should have called the House together immediately rather than creating additional problems in our economy by this delay.
Experience has shown that the government procrastinated last year during the railway strike, causing untold hardship to the economy in the very same way.
We should stop using parliament as a tool in labour-management disputes. We must put the interest of the public at large ahead of the narrow interests of two parties to a dispute. We must act to protect the public at large rather than one side or the other to a labour dispute. We 
must stop legislating the settlement of inflationary and politically expedient demands.
This parliament and its politicians should follow the advice given to the government in 1968 by implementing the recommendations of the Woods Commission. Unfortunately the government has failed to give leadership in any long-term sense, and has followed again the politically expedient course. It has added to inflationary expectations, and for that reason it would be impossible for me to support the inept handling of the situation suggested in the bill introduced by the government.

Mr. Speaker, while I hope to make a contribution at another time in another debate, since we have interrupted the debate on the Speech from the Throne I shall not take the time of the House, which is rather limited, to extend congratulatory messages to you and other hon. gentlemen who have already participated in that debate, because I want to keep basically to the issue, Bill C-12, designed to put the grain handlers in Vancouver back to work.
Without any ado, I wish to tell you, Mr. Speaker, and my colleagues in this House that this is a sad night in Canada when we begin to legislate Bill C-12 which, for the first time in Canadian parliamentary history, asks the parliament of Canada to decide to dot the i's and cross the t's in a labour contract.
This is a precedent which will come back to haunt this chamber, be it in the thirtieth parliament or in ensuing parliaments, because it is a wrong precedent. In the past we had proper precedents and necessary actions in a legislative way to get essential industries back to work. We convened parliament and parliament went to work without going into the issues under dispute between labour and management. What was done, and done reluctantly initially, was in a broad general way to appoint an arbitrator. Then the legislation in effect said that the people concerned should go back to work and that the arbitrator would rule on the issues in a just way, and adjudicate on merit, with fair play to both sides.
But here we have a government that was given a mandate on July 8. With all the momentum its majority mandate gives it, what does this government do? It makes Rip Van Winkle look like a piker with its dozing and snoozing.
Here we have the benevolent House leader, the hon. President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp), straight from the world of diplomacy. He comes to the floor of the House to help iron out some of the difficulties here. Mr. Speaker, if this is any indication of how this parliament will look as we continue our deliberations in the ensuing months, then all the minister's diplomatic prowess will be challenged because although we in this party intend to co-operate in
October 8, 1974

respect of legislation, we will not be used as a rubber stamp to make respectable something which is not respectable simply because this government slumbered for three months following the election.
I left my little home in the valley in Nova Scotia at 6.30 this morning and boarded a plane. I do not see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) here so I cannot congratulate him for Air Canada running on time. Finally I got here to this beautiful city. While the sun was lighting up the St. Lawrence and the beautiful country in that area I thought of several things. I thought with almost sadness: good gracious, why am I coming back to the city of Ottawa to become involved in an issue involving the west coast which has been considered by Dr. Perry and other people for months, people who understand the situation very well?
Is it not a sad commentary that the first item of legislation with which the government deals should be this blasphemous piece of legislation which parliament for the first time decides in its omnipotent wisdom to write into a contract?
I see my friend, a former minister, who used to practice a little labour law in the province of Manitoba, present in the House. I also see an authority on parliamentary procedure in this House who, even though he is along in chronological years, is young in heart and never abused the rules. He and his colleagues stand up in this House today and try to pick at Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition for opposing this bill. An hon. member I respect, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), said that because Dr. Perry thought the union should get most things, they will agree with the bill.

Think of the hypocrisy of the NDP in saying that because Dr. Perry gave this and this and this to the union, then this will be legislation in the public interest. I say this bill is not a blessing, Mr. Speaker, because of the precedent it sets. If this parliament is to write the detail of a contract it will be the first time for that to occur.
The things that give me more cause for concern are the contracts that have yet to go to collective bargaining and
Grain Handlers' Strike
those that are already in the collective bargaining process. Because of the precedent we are setting it is very likely they will end up on the floor of this chamber. I think that the new members of this House, who come here thinking they will be going to the core of issues before the country, helping to look after the economy, and who find themselves concerned with this bill as their piece of legislative business, will be disappointed.
Among the labour contracts coming up for renegotiation are those with the Cape Breton Development Corporation, Norando Mines Ltd., United Aircraft of Canada Ltd., Air Canada, the Maritime Employers' Association and the railways. Some, if not all of these are to be renegotiated by December 31.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to my hon. friends opposite that it is ridiculous for us to be setting this precedent tonight and having this bill as the first item of business in the thirtieth parliament. This government was given a majority by the Canadian people, and we have to accept that. That is the way the ball game is played and my leader will play fair. I will match him against any leader in this House. However, having set this precedent I predict that we will be known as "the parliament in labour" and no abortion bill is going to help this parliament. We are going to become befuddled, confused and over involved in the details of labour disputes that affect the national interest.
I am glad to see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) here tonight, Mr. Speaker. I think it was the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) who dubbed him and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) the Bobsey Twins, the Stardust Twins or something like that. There is no doubt that the intervention of the Minister of Labour is a serious matter, and we saw the power play of the minister when he told unions and management that they had better negotiate on the basis of the Perry report or parliament would be called back to pass legislation.

We were to have the Public Interest Disputes Commission, which is supposed to follow serious issues affecting labour-management relations in areas of public interest, on an ongoing basis. It would lance the boil that so often

rises in labour management disputes and sincere men, honestly differing, could have drawn the fester. I am not casting blame on the Vancouver grain handlers or on the elevator operators, Mr. Speaker.
The Perry report is not clear and it needs to be interpreted. Ad hoc, stop-start resolutions of disputes in the public service are just an insult to the parties involved, and indeed to all Canadians. I gather that the Minister of Labour is now expressing interest in a public disputes commission. Apparently he is going to call labour and management and other interested parties together to discuss the merits of collective bargaining procedures in an impasse.
The Liberal Party has been in power since 1963, Mr. Speaker,-and we still have the Minister of Labour, the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) and the other ministers who have been reshuffled. I point out to them that there are two basic tenets that must be part of any public interest disputes commission or any resolution of a contract. One is productivity and the other is participation.
I have full sympathy for all working men. We lag far behind other jurisdictions where the working man participates in the boardrooms and in management decisions. If students can picket universities and get a spokesman on the senate of universities, why cannot men, who have to earn their bread and butter through their work, have a voice in the boardrooms from time to time?
I think my friends opposite have said that we are the party of the establishment, but just look at the front benches over there, Mr. Speaker. They have either transplanted deputy ministers or some rogues from the St. James Street or Bay Street interests. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) can smile that smile that charmed the Arabs and the Jews. It did not produce any oil, however. He was deputy minister of finance and also of trade and commerce, and he dealt poker hands with the hoi polloi and nabods. That is why there is no concern for the working man.
The Postmaster General can scribble notes and give one of his speeches but it does not matter.
I say seriously, Mr. Speaker, that in labour-management discussions you have to have some type of measurement of productivity, and you also have to allow the working man some participation in management decisions. I go even further and say allow him some participation in the profits.
We have talked about the west coast but there is also a serious problem on the east coast. What has escaped the attention of this House and the country is that Thunder Bay and the Lakehead were closed by a strike on August 8. All movement of grain eastward from Thunder Bay was stopped until a few days ago when a new contract granting 65 per cent to 75 per cent over two years was signed with the Merchant Service Guild.
Where is the direction and leadership from this government to show whether labour contracts become inflationary or not? I suggest that if we set a precedent and agree to a settlement of between 65 and 75 per cent in an essential industry we will make the St. Lawrence Seaway settlement of 1966 look both like a pygmy and a piker compared with the wage scale being approved under this

contract. If we approve of inflationary settlements like this, what does it mean? The Speech from the Throne is meaningless if this type of contract is passed without comment. We hear talk about an excess profits tax. We should also talk about an excess wage settlement tax, which should be imposed on wage increases not linked to productivity increases.
On the east coast, because of the strike at the Lakehead, we have only about 20,000 or 30,000 bushels of grain. If during this winter the railways are beset by labour or weather problems, what will happen to our supplies in Atlantic Canada? The Grain Council in Atlantic Canada says we need 250,000 tons of grain, so that we will not have to kill our hens, our cattle and hogs because we cannot feed them. Unless we get grain our situation will be desperate.
That brings me to another point. We have fantastic elevator space in Atlantic Canada, yet speaker after speaker has said that we, in Atlantic Canada, need additional elevator capacity. Actually talks are going on right now about closing down our existing elevators, which have been used only to about 30 per cent of their capacity. What is wrong with the grain distribution system in Canada? We in the east need grain for domestic consumption and export, yet grain elevators we built have operated only at about 30 per cent of capacity during the last few years.

Mr. Speaker, the bill which was passed in the case of the rail strike contained provisions almost indentical to those contained in the report. That report had been rejected by the unions. If you look at the history of labour relations in this country, you find that parliament has been called into session immediately a rail strike occurs, and the legislation passed is legislation embodying suggestions which have previously been rejected by the trade unions. In the case I am talking about, a little over half of the unions' demands were dealt with by the report. Parliament was recalled within six weeks of the strike, as I recall.
Why are we dealing with this legislation now? Every day we spend debating this bill is costing the workers on the coast and farmers on the prairies thousands of dollars.
Grain Handlers' Strike
I submit that this is a futile exercise. We should end this debate as soon as possible.
I took exception to some remarks made yesterday by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) regarding this party and the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) who comes from Saskatchewan. The minister said that that hon. member is on top of his list for elimination. Yes, the old arrogance is back. The minister's attitude can best be described this way, "Today Saskatchewan; tomorrow the world". The power has gone to the minister's head. But the political world is very unsafe and I would not count chickens in Saskatchewan until all the eggs hatch.
There is an old axiom of trade unionism-no contract, no work. These grain handlers on the coast have been without a contract since November 30, 1973. They have really bent over backwards to accomodate this country in terms of service. To agree to what obviously is a settlement that is not acceptable to either party does no service to farmers on the prairies or workers on the coast. I must say that the directors of those elevator companies and co-ops have done no service to their farmers on the prairies by misrepresenting the facts in this case.
I refer particularly to United Grain Growers Limited which sent out wonderful material showing that the farmers overwhelmingly supported the position of United Grain Growers. If you examine that particular piece of guff, and that is the best description I can give it, it does not say anything about demurrage charges. It does not compare the cost of demurrage with the cost of settlement. The farmers were not given the full story. Those who work with their hands on the farm should have been invited to participate directly in those negotiations.
The negotiations have been poisoned for a very long time. A good example of that poison in the whole atmosphere was the decision of the grain firms to stop benefit payments following that strike. That is an almost unheard of act. It is an act of cruelty and vindictiveness. There is just no way you can expect a settlement in that atmosphere.
I do not agree with those who suggest that the decision by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) to say that the Perry report was supported by the government exacerbated this situation. There is no doubt that the grain workers were going to drop their tools and leave their employment at that time. That did not contribute to the problem.
The problem is that the Minister of Labour did not ask that parliament be called into session. I can understand why. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had a very trying election campaign. There is no doubt that he was tired and had to take it easy for about six weeks. We know what a great job he did in that campaign.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, after listening to the debate yesterday and today-

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: You learned something.

subtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO SECURE THE RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Yes, I did learn something. I learned that some do not have much to contribute. Some so-called experts have been disseminating nonsense. I can't learn from them.
There have been two outstanding areas of criticism. The first is that this is an inflationary settlement for which the government will have to take responsibility. The other is that the government, by identifying itself with the Perry recommendations, undermined the possibility of a settlement. I think these arguments are fallacious.
In closing I want to reiterate some of the principal points. First, dealing with the inflationary argument, there has been a propaganda effort put forward by some. This is certainly being done on the part of the companies involved. To a degree it is being mimicked and endorsed, I think ill-advisedly, by some members of the opposition. I am referring to this matter of an alleged 61 per cent settlement.
If there is a desire to try and establish a benchmark, it is to reiterate something like this. On any type of impartial examination, that is entirely false. It is not a 61 per cent settlement. Anyone who has had experience comparing various wage rates in various classifications, from data put out by the Department of Labour, Statistics Canada and others will know the comparisons. They compare all that unions with 500 or more employees have recently received in a collective bargaining session. They talk about wages. They do not include pensions, fringe benefits or other things won at the bargaining table, such as COLA.
This 61 percent figure includes all these. It is not accurate. It is excessive. If you want to compare it in terms of wage settlements won elsewhere, you must look at statistics. All you have to do is examine the record. It will show that this is marginally above an average of 15 per cent per year over a period of two years. That compares favourably with wage settlements on the west coast.
When you compare this wage settlement with all those other settlements, it stands up. Some of those other settle-

ments of 17 per cent a year, or 10 per cent a year, do not show all the fringe benefits that were won. In most cases some fringe benefits were won. They do not show pension concessions or COLA. Opposition members talk about wages. If you want to compare this wage settlement with others, you must be objective and fair. You must compare it on the basis as the comparisons are established. That does not include fringe benefits such as COLA or pensions. There we are talking in terms of a 15 per cent average per year.
I wish to emphasize one other point. If you wish to add all these other benefits, you should look at the companies' own figures. Presumably there will be an opportunity tomorrow in committee.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) talked about information sent out by United Grain Growers. It is quite true that they did not tell the farmers a lot of things. What they did tell them was inaccurate. They tried to get a response on what they did tell them. They talked about 61 per cent. It can be easily seen that they double counted the COLA clause. Would someone please tell me why it would be in the interests of the company to exaggerate a figure that even the union is not claiming? The union is prepared to sit down and say it is not 61 per cent. The union says there is double counting and it will accept a much lower figure. It is ridiculous to say it is still claiming a 61 per cent settlement.
I think this indicates to hon. members that the companies are not interested in settling this dispute. They want to make political marks if they can. They wish to embarrass the government. If they can get several allies in the official opposition to reiterate the falsification and the errors, they are going to do it. However, this is one of the matters to be examined by the committee tomorrow. We can point out the gross errors where the companies have intentionally, ill-advisedly, or unintentionally misinformed the farmers. This will be done on the basis of what they did tell them, let alone what they did not tell them.
The other reason given is that it seems inflationary. I ask hon. members opposite how it can be inflationary for Dr. Perry to have recommended for 550 grain handlers something less than 3,600 longshoremen have been receiving for the past year and a half, working side by side, and in many cases, doing the same work?
I have heard some members argue that grain handlers have a worse job than the longshoremen-it is dirty, it is dusty, it is harmful to the respiratory system, and so on. Yet these men have been paid comparatively less than longshoremen for a year and a half. And people call this settlement inflationary!
Do members opposite want to talk about percentages? I think it is idiotic to do so, because one ought to consider the equity involved in determining each particular case, and I have already given reasons for thinking there is a great deal of equity in this report of Dr. Perry. But when members opposite talk about the inflationary effect of a solution along those lines, I hear very little from them about the excess profits which are being made, the exorbitant return.', being gathered by some people, and about what some people outside the unions are making.
October 8, 1974

We don't hear anything about the professions, for example. We do not hear about what some of the executives are making. Why not? If members opposite are concerned about equity, why do they limit their concern about inflation to the effects of a settlement with 550 grain handlers? If they want to talk about combatting inflation, let them include everybody else. Let them include the professions and excess profits being made by certain corporate bodies.
If they want to talk that way, I am prepared to listen. But if they are only prepared to ensure grain handlers get less than those working beside them, all I can say is that I consider it to be a very anti-labour posture, and certainly an unjust posture.

I turn, now, to another aspect in terms of inflationary pressure. Many members of the opposition have sought to debunk the catch-up theory, and most unjustly, I think. The hon. member for Annapolis Valley, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alex-
Grain Handlers' Strike
ander) and others talked about the Lake Carriers' Association-the pilots and engineers. They spoke of a settlement involving 60 per cent or 65 per cent. Let them talk to many of the enlightened employers who voluntarily agreed to that settlement. I will tell them precisely what these employers will say, because my officials and I were involved for many days in the events surrounding that settlement. The employers agreed to that settlement on a voluntary basis.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext: You foisted it on them.

speechtext:
The outstanding reason was this: they were encountering manpower problems. They could not get second, third and fourth class engineers who had been trained for five or six years before getting their tickets, to be jacks of all trades and work for the same rates of pay as carpenters, electricians and so on. It is within this framework that, even in the absence of the unions, the employers would have found it necessary to concede significant increases to enable these men to catch up. Some of the members on the other side-I have in mind particularly, the hon. member for Hamilton West-were obviously not aware of this. To keep the industry viable, to keep the grain and the ore moving, they had to reach a settlement of that kind.
Today, when we are talking about grain handlers, the situation is the same. Unless the rates paid to these grain handlers, working under conditions deplorable as they are, are brought more into line with those paid to the longshoremen, I believe the companies will experience a great deal of difficulty in getting the manpower needed to man the operation.

speechtext: Give it a try.
