speechtext:
I am talking about paying realistic wage rates so as to get sufficient manpower to run the operation.
Now I should like to turn to another matter, and that is the whole question of whether we have, somehow, undermined the collective bargaining process by identifying with the Perry report. But first I wish to clear up one or two misconceptions.
The hon. member for Hamilton West asked why the union did not accept the Perry report after the government had identified itself with it. If he will check the facts he will find that the union did accept the Perry recommendations, and that the companies rejected them before the government became identified with the report.
Let me deal with yet another misconception advanced by the hon. member for Hamilton West. He sought to give the impression that the Perry report contained, not recommendations but suggestions-and that an attempt was being made to "put something over", or that some hanky-panky was involved here. If the hon. member would study the Labour Code he would realize that Dr. Perry had no other task but to bring in recommendations.
When a single commissioner brings in what he feels is a reasonable basis for a settlement, he is bringing in recommendations. That is what the statute calls for. And, once they are published, everyone knows exactly what they are. It is extremely naive for the hon. member or anyone else

October 8, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
to believe they could be interpreted as anything other than recommendations. Does one really expect a union leader to go to his membership and tell them not to pay any attention to them? How ludicrous, Mr. Speaker! These are recommendations. Dr. Perry was asked to bring in recommendations and, in fact, did bring in recommendations.
Let me come back to the charge that the government has undermined the collective bargaining process. When the companies came to Ottawa in May, before the government ever identified with the Perry recommendations, and we indicated that Dr. Perry had made certain recommendations, what did the companies and the union think about those recommendations?
We wondered whether they could arrive at some kind of settlement. It seemed that having made those recommendations they had to be taken seriously. But the companies said: "We are not going to accept the Perry recommendations as any type of basis for settlement. In fact, if we have no other alternative, there is going to be a work stoppage right away on that basis. There will have to be a work stoppage; we will have to have a strike or a lock-out".
Is that not indicative to hon. members that negotiation, bargaining, had completely broken down, and that an impasse had been reached? Of course that was the situation. What did the government do? When it had no alternative it had to implement section 188 of the Canada Labour Code and deny these workers the right to strike for up to three months. And not only that, it required them to work at the wage rate under the old collective bargaining agreement which expired in the previous November. It was already five months out of date and this added another three months to that.
Can any member of this House tell me that it would be fair and reasonable to expect those union leaders to require their workers to work under conditions like that without indicating to them what might be at the end of the road for them, especially when an independent report made by a third party was already made known? Would it be fair and reasonable, in anybody's estimation, to think that those workers could work under those conditions and would be prepared to do so? I ask each member to ask himself that question, and he will have to admit that the workers must be given some assurance. But this step avoided a breakdown of operations for three months.
This brings me to the point where the exercise of power under section 188 came to an end, which was roughly eight days after the return of the writs. I and my officials made every effort to try to reach a collective agreement. We tried, between the time when the power under section 188 expired and the time when the strike occurred on August 26, to reach agreement. Then after the lock-out or strike occurred we again tried right up until a week before the House came into session.
I ask hon. members; is that not what a Minister of Labour and his officials are supposed to do in a free collective bargaining system? Are they not supposed to make every effort possible to try to arrive at a settlement before using parliament to deny the rights of these workers? Some hon. members, the hon. member for Hamilton

West for one, and others, said that we should have called parliament into session very shortly after the strike occurred. Would we not then have been accused of acting arbitrarily and unnecessarily without making every effort to reach a settlement? Would we not have been accused of depriving these workers of their rights?
Did hon. members hear the union leaders and membership screaming for parliament to be called right after the strike occurred? They did not want parliamentary intervention; what they wanted was the collective bargaining system to be given a chance to work. They wanted to meet with the employers all through September and arrive at an agreement, and that is what should have happened. Those of us who believed in free collective bargaining made every possible effort to try to make it work before calling parliament.
All I am saying is that hon. members, such as the hon. member for Hamilton West and others, cannot complain on the one hand that we did not call parliament, which would have deprived these workers of their fundamental rights, and on the other hand say that we should not take away their bargaining rights but let the free collective bargaining system work. You cannot suck and whistle at the same time, but this is exactly what some members of the official opposition are trying to do on this particular issue.
During the course of this debate I have heard more reactionary, anti-labour speeches than I have heard in quite a long time. I was very surprised at how reactionary and anti-labour some hon. members can be in this situation when they hear the reasons why this particular report is justified. I suspect some members were quoting from company proposals and were urging them upon the House. I should like to read one viewpoint, if I may, expressed by one of the companies, the Palliser Wheat Growers. I am quoting their newsletter No. 33 for September, 1974:
As has happened too often in the past, the evertrusting grain grower, watching from the sidelines, will be the big loser. Those providing a service in the grains industry are playing loosely with the producers' livelihood as they endeavour to promote their own vested interest. We are painfully aware that the major costs of any settlement will be borne by the primary producer.
Then listen to this, Mr. Speaker:
We often cite wage settlements and rising prices as the main culprits in inflation; I suggest, however, that a contributing factor is the criminal waste that results from the non-productive use of capital equipment and manpower during the shutdown of an industry. It is unthinkable that responsible leaders in a so-called enlightened society will permit huge investments in ships, railway equipment, buildings, ports, and manpower as well, to stand idle while differences are settled.
I also refer to a report in the Regina Leader-Post headed "Saskatchewan groups want action in grain dispute". It quotes Mr. Nelson in the following terms:
Terming the present labour dispute-
That is a reference to the dispute with the grain companies.
-which has shut down grain exports from Vancouver the "farmer's own little Watergate," Mr. Nelson said grain company officials are guilty of "gross mismanagement and an irresponsible attitude."
There you have what one group thinks about this situation, Mr. Speaker. Also during this debate I have not heard very many members quote what the union has had to say.
October 8, 1974

Since I have heard what others have had to say, namely, the companies, perhaps it would not be out of order to put on the record what Mr. Kanes and the union have had to say, if for no other purpose than simply fundamental fairness. I am quoting from the brief that I believe was sent by local 333 to all members of parliament. Talking about the employers' campaign to discredit the Perry report, they say:
They have completely ignored the issue of parity of wages with the longshoring industry.
The brief goes on:
The grain workers are mindful of inflation as everybody is. But if the employers' argument had any validity the grain workers should not be awarded any increase whatsoever. Even a one-cent an hour increase would be inflationary.
We submit that the employers are raising a red herring, and grasping for public sympathy, when they talk about inflation. A settlement based on the Perry report will be inflationary only if the industry fails to take the necessary steps to increase productivity in grain handling.
The rest of the union's submission sets out in detailed fashion how it is prepared to co-operate in increasing productivity. After all we have heard about this inefficient industry, if the union is prepared to go on record as supporting increased productivity, and it gets co-operation from management in doing so, then this settlement may not be inflationary at all. I suggest we would then see a great increase in productivity.
One has only to trace the history of the negotiations that have taken place between the grain companies and the grain handlers over the past decade to realize why we are faced with this present situation. A history of the 1960's will show that three majority conciliation reports, signed by the chairmen, were rejected by the companies. In 1952 the late Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent in frustration wanted to take over the companies, and I quoted him in that reference. Again at that time it was the chairman's report which was rejected by the companies. We have witnessed an almost uninterrupted series of rejections. There have been settlements in intervening years, but when there has been a rejection of a report made by a third independent party, be it the report of a commissioner or the board chairman, it has been a rejection by the companies.
Is it any wonder that when members ask why we do not have a settlement in this particular situation, the more enlightened ones suggest that we go to the root of the causes of the disasters in management-labour relations in this industry? It is for this reason I have suggested the appointment of an industrial commission.
I have already given some indication of the history of what has happened, and of the efforts that have been expended to get to a settlement. When one goes a step further one must ask himself what other reason there can be for the situation other than the fact that ill will has been festering for years and years in terms of management-labour relations in this industry?
I strongly suspect that if any member of this House put himself into the role of a mediator trying to get a settlement he would like to think there was economic pressure
Grain Handlers' Strike
on both sides to settle. When there is such pressure the likelihood of reaching a settlement is much greater.
Do we have that kind of economic pressure on both sides to this dispute? Certainly the workers were on strike and were not drawing unemployment insurance benefits for five and a half or six weeks, so they were under pressure. What was the situation so far as the companies are concerned? Are they now under pressure? Perhaps if we look at that aspect of the matter we will find the key to why there has been no settlement here.
My friend and colleague, the minister responsible for the Wheat Board, indicated that the losses involved, even the demurrage charges, are not losses to the companies. These costs are passed on ultimately to the farmers. The companies are not paying any of the costs of this particular industrial relations fiasco. What is the pressure on the companies then to settle? I suggest this is a consideration we must take into account.
The companies do not have to pay the costs of this dispute. We now have a sellers' market. It has already been indicated that the companies are not terribly concerned about the employees. Keeping this in mind it is apparent that there is little motivation for the companies to settle. The companies are convinced that sooner or later they will sell the grain they now have on hand. In addition they know they will not have to pay the demurrage, so where is the pressure to settle? Why should they not turn down the report and use the whole thing politically to embarrass the government?
Every time a settlement is suggested the companies are tempted to embarrass the government and ridicule it across the country, even in the face of inflationary circumstances. The companies do not have to accept their responsibilities in arriving at a settlement. They do not even have to justify their actions to a membership, let alone the government. They use the government as an excuse for not accepting their own responsibilities. In addition to that the companies are able to get what I consider to be fairly enlightened members of the official opposition to buy their argument, hook line and sinker, and reiterate it, as they have done for the past two days.
If there is one question that should be asked during this debate it is whether some of these companies know what would be the entire cost of this settlement. I am referring to the cost of the settlement that could have been accepted at any time by the companies knowing full well, as every member of this House knows, that if parliament were recalled to settle the issue it must settle on the basis of other known precedents, and could not require the men to go back to work for anything less than the wage package recommended by the Perry report. I suggest everyone knows that. Everyone knows that there would not have been a settlement based on anything less than what was recommended in that report.
No one with any familiarity with the labour situation on the west coast would expect a settlement based on anything less than what was recommended by the independent third party, with any hope of ratification. Surely members of this House are not so naive as to think otherwise. In full awareness of some of these hypocrisies how can hon. members reiterate the nonsensical and idiotic things that have been said here for the last two days?

October 8, 1974

I suggested earlier that these companies should be asked whether they know what the cost of this settlement would have been. The entire cost of the settlement over the next two-year period would have been $2.5 million. If that is the case, how can these companies justify allowing these demurrage charges, which they will not have to pay, but which the farmers will have to pay, to reach $10 million? Is that an indication of responsibility on the part of the companies? Is it a sign of responsibility on the part of the companies to allow these deplorable employee-employer relationships to develop in this industry? subtopic: HEALTH-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL GOVERNMENT SHARING COST OF NURSING HOMES AND HOME CARE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
HEALTH-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL GOVERNMENT SHARING COST OF NURSING HOMES AND HOME CARE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day I asked the minister whether the federal government was considering cost sharing in respect of beds in chronic nursing homes as it does in the case of active treatment hospitals. It is my belief that the federal government is substantially adding to health costs by not accepting this proposal.
It must be remembered that the federal government brought in the so-called Hospital Insurance and Diagnos-
AcLjournment Debate
tic Services Act in 1957 whereby the federal government shared the cost of the program with the provinces. Each paid roughly about 50 per cent of the cost. At that time one could enter and leave hospital when the doctor felt that treatment so required. There were few if any chronic cases. The only exceptions were mental cases.
Extended health care did not come in until much later, when galloping health costs were swallowing up money faster than it could be budgeted. Hospital costs under the national health plan have risen from $20 per bed per day to $100 per bed per day in a period of about 15 years. In other words, the cost has risen five times in less than 15 years.
Health care costs are increasing at twice the rate of the gross national product. Surely no loopholes should be left unguarded. The cost now in Ontario has reached the astronomical figure of $2 billion. It is estimated, at the present rate, that in ten years it will be over $11 billion.
This could be a serious factor because health care may be cut in a very sensitive area which, in the long run, would cost much more. A patient who goes into an active treatment hospital today may be ready for discharge in two or three weeks. He may be able to return to his home if there is anyone there to care for him, or arrangements may be made for a homemaker to go to his home. The unfortunate thing is that the homemaker remains in the home for eight hours or less a day, which means that the patient is alone for a period of 16 hours unless he has relatives or friends to look after him. This type of home care service is completely inadequate.
What is required is that someone live in the patient's home until the patient has improved sufficiently to look after himself. This is not adequately funded. If a patient at the end of that treatment must go to an after-care facility, or extended care facility, there is a roadblock. In many cases a period of days or weeks expires before such a patient can get accommodation in an extended care bed.
There are not sufficient beds. We must have more facilities of this type. Such facilities could look after chronic cases exceptionally well. The nurses and associated workers become adept at looking after such patients.
Now we hear talk about cutting costs. Here is an ideal place to do it. An active treatment bed costs perhaps as high as $100 per day, while an extended care bed costs $17 per day. A patient could stay for a period of five days in an extended care facility for what it would cost to stay one day in an active treatment bed. In Canada there are nearly 1300 hospitals with 146,000 beds. If a patient could be sent to a health care nursing home, there would be a saving of two days in hospital per patient. This would lower costs and not interfere with the efficiency of care. The proportion of the cost in respect of building homes of this type will become greater and these homes will become more and more crowded as more and more people enter the older age group.
The age group from 65 up is the fastest growing in the country. It is the group that incurs shortened and less acute illness, and more and more chronic vascular disease and degenerative disease. It is to care for those people with adequate facilities that we must prevent cut-backs. To cut back would be a retrograde step in the health field.

October 8, 1974
Adjournment Debate
The minister has accepted responsibilities in respect of some extended care facilities, and I now ask him to accept his responsibilities in providing health care not only for the acutely ill but for the chronically ill, that is, all those requiring extended care. Then he will have accepted the principle that surely is fundamental: that the most serious thing of all to any person is a long drawn out illness, often without hope of rehabilitation. It is for those people that I make this plea tonight.

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL GOVERNMENT SHARING COST OF NURSING HOMES AND HOME CARE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am informed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) that the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) is well known in this House when it comes to matters of health. It is a pleasure for me to reply to such a notable health critic.
The government is well aware of the matter of rising health costs. It is aware of the way in which the present cost sharing programs encourage the continued use of high cost services, such as active treatment beds, when services like nursing homes or home care programs might well suffice. It is for this reason that the federal government proposed at the federal-provincial conference of ministers of health in May, 1973, a health cost financing formula.
The formula recognized the need to afford to provinces a greater flexibility in the determination of their priorities, as well as recognizing the importance of creating the incentive and the means to rationalize the health care system as a whole. At that time the provinces did not commit themselves to this formula, pending further study. It now appears that the provinces do not accept the proposed formula. The federal government is awaiting new proposals on the alternative solutions they would suggest.
The hon. member is aware that sharing in the cost of nursing home care is available under the Canada Assistance Plan where care is provided to persons in need. The department announced in February, 1974, that the government would be prepared to continue sharing where provinces choose to introduce programs based on the universal availability of the benefit. A measure to this effect is expected to be introduced this session to authorize such sharing in respect to the provinces of Ontario, Manitoba and Alberta, which have, to date, introduced universal nursing home care programs.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-ALLEGED ACTION OF LAURENTIAN PILOTAGE AUTHORITY CHANGING BASIS FOR PILOT'S CERTIFICATE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
TRANSPORT-ALLEGED ACTION OF LAURENTIAN PILOTAGE AUTHORITY CHANGING BASIS FOR PILOT'S CERTIFICATE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on October 2, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marc-hand)-who has been good enough to remain here this evening and I want to thank him for that-in answer to my question on when the Desjardins report commissioned by him pursuant to section 14(5) of the Pilotage Act would be made public, replied "-as soon as we complete its study".
That is fair enough, Madam Speaker, but while this study is proceeding there are a few more questions that I hope will be taken under advisement and answered by the minister.

First and foremost, why has the government in its wisdom given the pilotage authorities the complete and total power to regulate the issuance of pilotage certificates? If you stop to examine the logic here, it makes as much sense as designing a parachute which will open on impact.
Without in any way blaming the Laurentian Pilotage Authority, which after all will naturally do its best to extend its influence, it must be remembered that the pilotage authorities in this country set examination standards, conduct examinations, and have complete and total control over whether a certificate is issued. It is obvious and elementary that it is not in the interests of a pilotage authority to issue great numbers of pilotage certificates. The issuance of each certificate reduces the income of the pilots in the area in question. I would ask the minister to change this rather extraordinary situation by making the necessary statutory amendments.
The next question I ask is: why did the Laurentian Pilotage Authority take the step it did in changing the basis for issuing pilotage certificates? Was this a quid pro quo, or an inducement, or one of the reasons for their settling the labour dispute last spring? I hope not, because such a suggestion would have cynical overtones.
Further to this line of reasoning, which I hope is not correct, can it be that the unusual conditions implicit in the Desjardin inquiry are designed to expedite the acceptance of the amendment? I say this because two of the conditions are somewhat unusual. For instance, condition No. 2 says:
The investigation shall not be subject to the customary rules of evidence nor need evidence be taken under oath.
As a lawyer I find that strange. Condition No. 3 specifies that:
The investigation shall not be conducted by means of public hearings but, on the contrary, through the investigation and examinations of those persons whom the said investigator deems possessed of evidence relevant to the subject matter and whose evidence should be examined in the public interest.
Another important issue concerns the opinion written by Professor W. R. Lederman, Professor of Law at Queen's University. Professor Lederman is a nationally recognized constitutional expert. In his opinion what is being proposed is unconstitutional.
Let me also ask this question. Does the proposed amendment help in any meaningful way to improve the safety, efficiency or economy of marine transportation. I believe the sooner these and other questions are answered, the better it will be for all concerned.
I want to see the Laurentian Pilotage Authority do well. I was one of those who supported their bid for parity with their west coast brethren in the Pacific coast pilotage authority when they encountered difficulty last spring in labour negotiations. There is an important issue at stake. The rights of others are involved, as well as the efficiency of our transportation system. The determination of those rights may depend on the contents of the Desjardin report.
I urge the minister, because of the importance of this matter, to begin this new session of parliament on a
October 8, 1974

constructive note. Let him bring this report forward quickly and deal with it.

subtopic: RESEARCH-NEED FOR ADDITIONAL FUNDS IN MEDICAL FIELD-NUMBER OF SCIENTISTS LEAVING CANADA BECAUSE OF LACK OF FUNDS

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: RESEARCH-NEED FOR ADDITIONAL FUNDS IN MEDICAL FIELD-NUMBER OF SCIENTISTS LEAVING CANADA BECAUSE OF LACK OF FUNDS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the matter I bring to the adjournment debate this evening is one of mounting urgency and importance. I thank the minister for the tone of his reply when I asked him yesterday if he had been able to find the additional $2.5 million for the Medical Research Council since his undertaking to try to do so earlier this year. However, I also want to say how profoundly disappointed I was with the content of his response, that he had not been successful in his efforts.
The amount we are talking about, $2.5 million, is not large when one considers that the departments' overall budget is almost $5 billion. However, it is an extremely critical amount, not only to our scientific community but in determining the future standard of health care for all Canadians.
Earlier this year there was considerable discussion in committee and testimony provided by expert witnesses to substantiate the crying need for additional funding in medical research. At that time it was stated, and I quote:
Since a nation's health is basic to its economy, biomedical science policies should be the concern of every Canadian. The presence of a crisis in a small area of government concern which may have a very large effect on our nation should be recognized now before matters go beyond a state of repair.
The plea was made to abandon the on-again, off-again style of nourishing research in Canada. Economists are agreed that any viable industry spends about 4.5 per cent on basic and marketing research. The biomedical sciences are not even asking for 2 per cent of its industry's budget. They are pleading against further erosion.
The government's decision to grant only a small increase in last year's budget to MRC and subsequently to hold the line on this year's figure has not only deprived medical research of a realistic increase in funds, but as well subjected existing funds to serious erosion by twodigit inflation. The situation was deemed critical by many concerned Canadians last spring, and the intervening months have seen a continuing deterioration.
In June a joint statement was issued by the Canadian Society for Clinical Investigation, the Canadian Federation of Biological Societies and the Association of Canadian Medical Colleges which pointed out, and I quote:
In some medical schools, research programs in clinical departments are shrinking or closing down entirely because, in the absence of council support, they have no source of funds. Potential researchers are discouraged from entering upon a research career and the continuance of research activities by existing medical scientists is threatened.
Since then numerous representations have been made to me pointing out that certain projects are grinding to a halt because mounting inflation makes it impossible to absorb increased costs from funds made available even earlier this year.

October 8, 1974
Adjournment Debate
Recently the Medical Research Council announced that it does not have adequate funds to support the project of a computerized pancreas, a project which has potential benefit for thousands of Canadian diabetics.
The greatest potential for disaster in the government's niggardly commitment to medical research is its impact on young graduates contemplating research careers. Last year only one per cent of the graduating class in one of our leading medical schools planned to enter a career in biomedical research and teaching, as compared with 10 per cent as recently as 1969. The appalling attrition in recruitment for medical research is understandable, given the vulnerability of the future of medical research, but it can have disastrous consequences for future generations of Canadians.
I plead with the minister and his colleagues to remove the constraints which were placed on medical research earlier this year, and to ensure that future budgets will include a constant dollar application and a realistic and guaranteed percentage of total health costs for research.

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: RESEARCH-NEED FOR ADDITIONAL FUNDS IN MEDICAL FIELD-NUMBER OF SCIENTISTS LEAVING CANADA BECAUSE OF LACK OF FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 7, in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) undertook to determine whether such a study had been carried out.
Inquiries were made and, as far as can be determined, no study has been undertaken or is under way to attempt to tabulate the number of medical scientists who have left Canada to pursue their research in another country.
Even if this number were to be known, the reasons which led these individuals to decide to leave would, of course, be difficult to determine. Further, in order to balance the books one would have to determine the numbers who have come to Canada and their reasons for doing so. Personally I do not think that the number of medical scientists who have left Canada because they felt their research would receive better support in another country, and for whom this was a major reason for their decision to emigrate, has been significant. However, as I have said, no serious attempts appear to have been made to determine this number, nor do I think there is any practical way of determining the motives of those who may have left.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I should like to repeat the minister's undertaking to seek out any funds which may be surplus to existing programs in his department so that he may transfer them to the Medical Research Council before the end of the fiscal year.
